lessons.title: The Great American Desert and Manifest Destiny

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question, do not list everything Manifest Destiny was — the examiner has read the spec. Pick two or three precise effects and link each one through a clear chain. For example: ‘Because the doctrine framed expansion as a divine duty, Polk could win the 1844 election on a programme of acquiring Texas and Oregon, which led directly to war with Mexico in 1846, which in turn delivered the lands of the Mexican Cession in 1848.’ That is the analytical chain top answers build.
before.content_html:
A Continent Mostly Unknown

In 1840 the United States stretched from the Atlantic to the Mississippi, but most Americans had never set foot west of that great river. Beyond it lay a continent few easterners could picture clearly. The land rose from rolling prairies to the vast, treeless Great Plains, climbed sharply into the Rocky Mountains, and finally fell away through deserts and mountain ranges to a fertile Pacific coast. Rivers were few; rainfall west of the 100th meridian was unreliable; and timber, the staple building material of the East, ran out somewhere around the Missouri.

In 1820 the army explorer Stephen Long crossed the Plains and produced an influential map. He stamped the words ‘Great American Desert’ across the heart of the continent and concluded the region was “almost wholly unfit for cultivation, and of course uninhabitable by a people depending upon agriculture”. For the next twenty years schoolbooks repeated the verdict. The Plains were a barrier to be crossed, not a place to live.

Key Fact

Stephen Long’s 1820 expedition labelled the Plains the ‘Great American Desert’ on US maps. The verdict shaped policy until the 1840s, when settlers began to see the same land as a route to the fertile West Coast rather than a barrier.

Why the ‘Desert’ Idea Began to Crack

By the 1840s the East was changing fast. Cities were crowded with immigrants, the 1837 financial panic had thrown thousands of farmers off their land, and soils in New England and the Atlantic states were exhausted after generations of cropping. Pull factors became powerful: missionaries returning from Oregon described its rich valleys; California offered a Mediterranean climate and good harbours; and gold strikes after 1848 made the journey suddenly worth the risk. The Plains were no longer a destination but a gateway.

Coining Manifest Destiny

In July 1845 the editor John O’Sullivan published an article in the New York newspaper the Democratic Review arguing that the United States had “the right of our manifest destiny to overspread and to possess the whole of the continent which Providence has given us”. The phrase caught on instantly. It bundled together three older ideas Americans had held for decades: a religious sense that God favoured the United States; a racial belief in the superiority of Anglo-Saxonism; and a political confidence that republican institutions were the best in the world.

Importantly, ‘manifest’ meant obvious or beyond argument, and ‘destiny’ meant divinely fixed. Together the words declared that westward expansion was not a choice; it was a duty. Anyone who stood in the way — Mexicans south of the border, British settlers in Oregon, the Plains nations — was, on this logic, opposing the will of Providence itself.

Push factors drove people away from the East: overcrowded cities, the 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion, and (for groups like the Mormons) religious persecution. Pull factors drew them west: cheap or free land in Oregon and California, gold strikes after 1848, missionary reports of fertile valleys, and the promise of a fresh start. Manifest Destiny linked the two by giving migration a moral meaning — settlers were not running from failure; they were carrying American civilisation across the continent.

From Idea to Policy

Manifest Destiny was a slogan, but it shaped concrete decisions almost at once. President James K. Polk, elected in 1844, came to office promising to acquire Texas, Oregon and California. The 1845 annexation of Texas sparked the Mexican-American War (1846–48). Victory and the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) added a vast territory — the present-day states of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and parts of Colorado and Wyoming. The Louisiana Purchase of 1803 had already doubled the country; in less than five years Polk doubled it again.

Manifest Destiny also shaped attitudes towards the people already living on the land. The doctrine treated North America as if it were empty waiting room, but the Plains were home to hundreds of thousands of Native people in dozens of nations. The historian Patricia Nelson Limerick has argued that Manifest Destiny’s real role was not to describe a vacuum but to legitimise dispossession — to make the removal and confinement of those nations look natural and good. That long shadow fell over every later policy in this unit.

One reading, dominant for most of the 20th century, presented westward expansion as the engine of American democracy — a frontier that toughened settlers and produced free institutions. A second, revisionist reading from the late 1980s onwards reframed the same story as a process of conquest, in which religion and race were used to justify taking land from people already on it. The two readings often appear in interpretation questions: top answers explain why each writer reaches a different verdict, not just what each one says.

Key Fact

Manifest Destiny had three major consequences in the 1840s alone: war with Mexico (1846–48); the gain of vast new territory through the Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848); and a sharper, more confident push of settlers and policy onto land already occupied by Native nations.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the idea of Manifest Destiny on US policy in the 1840s.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked back to Manifest Destiny through an explicit causal chain; precise factual support (Polk’s 1844 election, Texas annexation 1845, Mexican-American War 1846–48, Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo 1848).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal linking.
Developing: Effects identified but partly described rather than explained; thin causal links.
Emerging: Generalised statements about expansion without clear effects or links.

Indicative content:
• Polk’s presidential platform (1844) made acquiring Texas, Oregon and California explicit policy.
• Annexation of Texas (1845) and the Mexican-American War (1846–48) were justified as carrying out a manifest duty.
• The Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo (1848) added the present-day states of California, Nevada, Utah, Arizona, New Mexico and parts of Colorado and Wyoming.
• The doctrine hardened attitudes to the Plains nations: their land was treated as already destined to be American.

practice_questions.text:
Has the idea of Manifest Destiny been the most important reason for westward expansion in the 1840s?

• Manifest Destiny
• Push and pull factors

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Manifest Destiny against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support across both bullets and other relevant material; examiner-style judgement (e.g. ‘the doctrine was decisive because it converted material push factors into a sense of moral duty’).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement made.
Developing: Both bullets covered but treated as a list rather than weighed; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet covered or general narrative without judgement.

Indicative content:
• Manifest Destiny: O’Sullivan 1845, Anglo-Saxonism, Providence, Polk’s 1844 election platform, justification for Mexican-American War.
• Push and pull factors: 1837 Panic, soil exhaustion, urban overcrowding, Oregon valleys, gold strikes, religious freedom for Mormons.
• Other relevant material: improved transport (steamboats, early railroads), missionary reports, treaty acquisitions (Louisiana 1803, Texas 1845, Oregon 1846).
• Judgement: top answers argue that material factors created the demand, but Manifest Destiny supplied the moral cover that turned migration into national policy.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of geography on American attitudes to the West before 1845.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects of the physical geography on attitudes, with precise detail (Long 1820, ‘Great American Desert’ label, school maps, the role of the 100th meridian, scarce timber and water); explicit causal links.
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal links.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements about geography without explaining attitudes.

Indicative content:
• Stephen Long’s 1820 expedition stamped ‘Great American Desert’ on official maps, shaping policy and schoolbook geography for two decades.
• Lack of timber, water and reliable rainfall west of the Mississippi made eastern farming methods look impossible.
• The Rockies and the Sierras were treated as barriers to be crossed quickly, encouraging a focus on the Pacific coast as the real prize.
• These attitudes only began to shift in the 1840s when push and pull factors and missionary reports recast the Plains as a route, not a destination.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of Manifest Destiny.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a school textbook published in 1893.
“The frontier was the gift of America to the world. Each new acre opened in the West renewed the energies of the Republic and offered a fresh chance to honest, hardworking men.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a university history textbook published in 1990.
“Manifest Destiny dressed up dispossession in the language of duty. Beneath the rhetoric of God and Providence lay a simple fact: someone already lived on the land that was being claimed.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, precisely-supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support from each interpretation.
Developing: One clear difference; second weak or repetitive.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone without specific differences.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 presents Manifest Destiny as a positive force (‘gift to the world’) while Interpretation 2 presents it as a justification for harm (‘dispossession’).
• Interpretation 1 focuses on the white male settler experience; Interpretation 2 foregrounds the people already living on the land.
• Interpretation 1 frames expansion in moral and patriotic terms; Interpretation 2 strips away the moral language to describe a transfer of land.
• Interpretation 1 stresses opportunity and renewal; Interpretation 2 stresses cost and concealment.

practice_questions.text:
Why might the two interpretations of Manifest Destiny in the previous question give different views?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Explanation focuses on authors’ purpose, audience, time of writing or evidence used; supported by precise contextual knowledge of historiographical change.
Secure: At least one clear reason rooted in provenance or context, briefly supported.
Developing: Reason given but slips into ‘how’ rather than ‘why’.
Emerging: Restates what each interpretation says.

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: Interpretation 1 is from 1893, the Frontier Thesis era when expansion was celebrated; Interpretation 2 is from 1990, after revisionist scholarship that foregrounded conquest and Native experience.
• Audience and purpose: a 19th-century school textbook was meant to build patriotism; a late-20th-century university text was meant to challenge inherited stories.
• Evidence: writers in 1893 had little access to Native voices; writers in 1990 could draw on tribal histories and 20th-century scholarship.
• Top answers explain WHY the two writers reach different verdicts, not what each verdict is.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the geography of North America that shaped attitudes to westward expansion before 1845.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct features, each developed with at least one precise factual point.
Secure: Two valid features with brief support.
Developing: Two features identified but one undeveloped.
Emerging: One feature only or generalised description.

Indicative content:
• The Great Plains: a vast treeless grassland west of the Mississippi, labelled the ‘Great American Desert’ on the 1820 Long map and seen as too dry for eastern-style farming.
• The Rocky Mountains: a high north-south barrier with few passes, making the journey slow and dangerous and reinforcing the idea that the West Coast, not the interior, was the real destination.
• Rivers and rainfall: scarce reliable water west of the 100th meridian made established eastern farming methods look impossible.
• The Pacific coast: fertile valleys (e.g. the Willamette in Oregon) and natural harbours pulled settlers across the continent rather than tempting them to settle the Plains.

lessons.title: Brigham Young and the Mormon Migration

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on the Mormons, resist the temptation to write everything you know in date order. The examiner is looking for two or three precise effects of Young’s leadership or the Salt Lake settlement, each linked through ‘this meant that’ or ‘as a result’. A clean structure: pick effect, give a precise fact (e.g. the company-of-fifty system), then explain the consequence (low death rate compared with secular trails), then move on. Three short paragraphs of analysis beats a long retelling of the trek.
before.content_html:
A New Religion in a Hostile East

In 1830 a young man from upstate New York, Joseph Smith, published the Book of Mormon and founded a new church — the Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints. Smith claimed an angel had revealed golden plates with the lost gospel of an ancient American people. The new faith grew quickly, but it also collected enemies. Mormons believed they were God’s gathered people, voted as a bloc, refused to mix religion and the state in the way most Americans expected, and from the late 1830s a small minority practised polygamy. Each move — from New York to Ohio, then Missouri, then Nauvoo in Illinois — ended with their neighbours driving them out.

Key Fact

Joseph Smith was murdered by a mob at Carthage, Illinois on 27 June 1844. After a brief power struggle, Brigham Young emerged as the new leader and decided the Saints could not survive within the United States as it then was — they needed a place no one else wanted.

Brigham Young Takes Over

Smith’s death left around 12,000 Saints in Nauvoo facing a hostile state government. Brigham Young was a former carpenter and senior apostle. He was a brilliant organiser rather than a mystic, and within months he had a plan: leave the United States entirely and build a new society in Mexican territory beyond the Rockies. Young chose the Great Salt Lake Valley because the explorer John C. Fremont had described it as fertile but uninhabited, and because nobody else wanted it — it sat in a high desert with bitter winters and unreliable water.

The Mormon Trail, 1846–47

In February 1846 the Saints began crossing the frozen Mississippi out of Nauvoo. Young drilled them like an army. Wagon trains were divided into companies of fifty, each with a captain, and into groups of ten, each with a captain. He published travel rules, set times for prayer, food and rest, and ordered that crops be planted at staging posts so later companies could eat. The first 1846 winter was spent in temporary settlements at Winter Quarters on the Missouri, where roughly 600 died of cold, scurvy and disease. The advance pioneer party of 148 set out in April 1847 and reached the Salt Lake Valley on 24 July 1847. Young, ill with fever, lifted his head from the wagon, looked across the valley and famously said, “This is the right place. Drive on.”

The Mormon Trail ran roughly 1,300 miles from Nauvoo to the Salt Lake Valley. Young’s organisation was strikingly different from the typical California-bound wagon train. Companies stuck together rather than racing each other. Sick travellers were cared for by the whole company, not abandoned. Tools, seeds and breeding livestock were shared. Crops planted at staging stops fed later groups. The trail kept moving for years — by 1869, when the railroad replaced wagons, around 70,000 Saints had crossed it. The collective discipline meant a remarkably low death rate compared with secular trails such as the Oregon and California Trails.

Building Deseret

The Mormons called their new home Deseret, a Book of Mormon word meaning ‘honeybee’ — an emblem of co-operative work. Within hours of arrival the pioneers were already digging the first irrigation ditches, redirecting mountain streams to soak the dry valley floor. Young laid out Salt Lake City on a strict grid, with ten-acre blocks, wide streets and a central temple square. Land was held by the church and assigned to families based on what they could work, not what they could pay; water rights belonged to communities, not individuals. New arrivals were directed to one of the satellite settlements (Ogden, Provo, Manti) so the colony could spread without fragmenting.

Crops failed in the first summer of 1848 when a plague of crickets devoured the wheat. According to Mormon tradition, vast flocks of seagulls arrived from the Great Salt Lake and ate the crickets, saving the harvest. Whatever the explanation, the colony survived, and by 1850 around 11,000 Saints were settled in Deseret. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo had quietly transferred the territory from Mexico to the United States — the very government Young had hoped to escape was now once again his neighbour.

Three factors stand out. First, leadership: Young combined religious authority with practical organisation, so individuals followed orders during the trek and the early settlement. Second, unity: shared faith and shared persecution made the Saints willing to share land, water and labour. Most other migrant groups were collections of strangers chasing private profit, especially miners. Third, geography: the Salt Lake Valley was so isolated that no other settler group fought them for it for over a decade. Tom and Mike on Oregon-bound trails arrived as individuals; Young arrived as a society.

Key Fact

The Mormon settlement worked because three things came together: tightly organised leadership under Brigham Young; collective ownership of land and water through the church; and the geographic isolation of a valley nobody else wanted — until 1848, when the United States acquired it from Mexico.

A Peace That Would Not Last

For the first decade Deseret was almost a separate country. Young served as territorial governor from 1850, and church and state ran together. But polygamy, theocratic government and the Saints’ refusal to obey federal officials produced steadily worsening relations with Washington. The story would end badly for some — the Mountain Meadows Massacre of 1857 (covered in lesson 13) — and would force the United States to confront the question of whether religious community could trump federal law. For now, though, the achievement was unmistakable: in just three years, a community driven out of the East had built a working society in a desert.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Brigham Young’s leadership on the Mormon migration of 1846–47.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects of Young’s leadership, each linked back through an explicit causal chain; precise factual support (companies of fifty, ten captains, planted crops at staging posts, low death rate, Salt Lake arrival 24 July 1847).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail and some causal linking.
Developing: Effects identified but partly described rather than explained.
Emerging: Generalised statements about the trek without clear effects.

Indicative content:
• Tight organisation: companies of fifty and ten with named captains gave the trek a chain of command, which meant orders were obeyed even in crisis.
• Shared supplies and crops planted at staging posts meant later companies could eat, lowering the death rate compared with the secular Oregon Trail.
• Choosing the Salt Lake Valley meant settling somewhere no one else wanted, removing competition for land in the early years.
• Religious authority gave Young the power to enforce decisions that purely civil leaders could not, holding the community together when 600 died at Winter Quarters.

practice_questions.text:
Compare the following two interpretations of the Mormon settlement of Utah.

Interpretation 1: An extract from a popular American history written in 1925.
“The Mormons in Utah are the supreme example of pioneer self-help. Driven out of the East, they crossed a continent and turned a desert into a garden through faith and hard work.”

Interpretation 2: An extract from a 2008 academic essay on the American West.
“The Mormon project succeeded because Brigham Young built a tightly disciplined community in which land, water and even marriage were controlled by the church. It was less an example of frontier individualism than of organised theocracy.”

Identify two ways in which the interpretations are different.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, supported differences drawn from both interpretations.
Secure: Two valid differences with brief support.
Developing: One clear difference; second weak.
Emerging: Vague comment about tone.

Indicative content:
• Interpretation 1 stresses self-help and individualism; Interpretation 2 stresses central control and theocracy.
• Interpretation 1 emphasises faith and hard work; Interpretation 2 emphasises institutional power over land, water and marriage.
• Interpretation 1 frames the achievement as American pioneer typical; Interpretation 2 frames it as unusual and organised, even un-American by frontier standards.
• Interpretation 1 is celebratory; Interpretation 2 is analytical.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of polygamy on relations between the Mormons and other Americans by 1857.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two or three developed effects, each linked through a clear chain; precise factual support (1852 public announcement, federal officials, hostile press, build-up to Mountain Meadows in 1857).
Secure: Two clear effects with relevant detail.
Developing: Effects identified but description-heavy.
Emerging: General statements without explaining the consequences.

Indicative content:
• The 1852 public announcement of polygamy by Brigham Young intensified hostility from churches and newspapers in the East, painting Mormons as un-American.
• Federal officials sent to Utah resigned or were driven out, prompting Washington to send troops in 1857 (Utah War).
• Polygamy provided political ammunition against statehood: Utah would not be admitted to the Union until 1896, after polygamy was officially renounced.
• The hostility created a siege mentality that helps explain the violent overreaction at Mountain Meadows in September 1857.

practice_questions.text:
Has Brigham Young’s leadership been the main reason the Mormons succeeded in Utah?

• Brigham Young’s leadership
• Geographic isolation of the Salt Lake Valley

Explain your answer with reference to both bullet points and other relevant information.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs Young’s leadership against geography (and other factors), reaching a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support across both bullets and additional material.
Secure: Clear argument addressing both bullets and at least one other factor; judgement reached.
Developing: Both bullets covered as a list; judgement implicit.
Emerging: One bullet only or general narrative.

Indicative content:
• Young’s leadership: company-of-fifty system; planted crops at staging posts; grid plan of Salt Lake City; church-controlled land and water; theocratic governance from 1850.
• Geographic isolation: high desert valley nobody else wanted; protected from settler competition for over a decade; bitter winters made independent survival a community task.
• Other relevant material: shared faith and persecution; collective ownership of resources; the ‘miracle of the gulls’ in 1848; Mormon willingness to follow orders.
• Judgement: top answers argue that isolation gave Young the chance to build a society, but his leadership turned that chance into success. Without either factor the project would have failed.

practice_questions.text: Describe two features of the Mormon settlement of the Salt Lake Valley.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct, developed features with precise factual detail.
Secure: Two valid features with brief support.
Developing: One feature developed; one undeveloped.
Emerging: Generalised description.

Indicative content:
• Irrigation: pioneers diverted mountain streams onto the valley floor within hours of arrival, making farming possible in a high desert.
• City planning: Salt Lake City was laid out on a strict grid with ten-acre blocks and a central temple square.
• Church control of land: families were allocated plots based on what they could work, not what they could pay, with water rights held communally.
• Satellite settlements: new arrivals were directed to towns like Ogden, Provo and Manti, allowing the colony to spread without fragmenting.

practice_questions.text:
Why might historians give different views of the Mormon migration?

Use Interpretations 1 and 2 (above) and your contextual knowledge to explain your answer.
practice_questions.marks:

Indicative content:
• Time of writing: a 1925 popular history reflects an inter-war Frontier-Thesis culture that celebrated pioneer individualism; a 2008 academic essay reflects modern scholarship interested in institutions and power.
• Audience: a popular history wanted patriotic stories; an academic essay wanted to explain causes precisely.
• Evidence: by 2008 historians had access to detailed records of the church’s economic role; in 1925 the available materials emphasised the dramatic trek.
• Purpose: one celebrates; the other analyses.

lessons.title: Pioneer Farmers, the Journey West and the Miners

before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Period Essay, covering both bullets is the floor, not the ceiling. The top band rewards a substantiated overall judgement. On a question comparing the impact of pioneer farmers with the impact of miners, ask yourself: which group changed the West faster, and which more deeply? Farmers built towns slowly over decades; miners flooded California overnight. Pick a side, argue it through, and give the examiner a closing sentence that names the verdict explicitly.
before.content_html:
Why Farmers Went West

Long before gold dominated the headlines, the great force pushing Americans westward was hunger for land. East-coast soils had been farmed for two centuries; in places they were exhausted. The 1837 Panic, a sharp banking crisis, drove thousands of indebted farmers off their plots, while immigration from Ireland and Germany was crowding eastern cities. Beyond the Mississippi, by contrast, lay vast tracts of fertile valley land in Oregon and California — territory the United States did not yet control but that missionary reports described in glowing terms. The first pioneer wagon trains for Oregon set out in 1841; by 1846, when Britain ceded the Oregon Territory south of the 49th parallel, the trickle had become a flow.

Key Fact

The Oregon Trail (used heavily from 1841) and the California Trail (especially from 1849) both began at Independence, Missouri and ran roughly 2,000 miles west. Pioneer farmers were pushed by soil exhaustion and the 1837 Panic, and pulled by the fertile Willamette Valley and free or cheap land.

The Wagon Train

Most pioneer farmers travelled in wagon trains — columns of fifteen to fifty covered wagons that gathered each spring at Independence, Missouri. Wagons were small (around four feet wide and ten feet long), pulled by oxen rather than horses because oxen ate prairie grass and could pull heavier loads, and packed with tools, seeds, flour, bacon, dried fruit and a little furniture. Families walked beside their wagons rather than rode in them. Each train elected a captain who set the pace, decided when to camp and resolved disputes. The journey took four to six months and had to be completed before the autumn snows closed the mountain passes.

Hardships on the Trail

The dangers were real, though students sometimes overstate the role of Native attacks. Far more migrants died of cholera, typhoid and dysentery picked up at riverside campsites where dirty water mixed with human waste. Accidents — children run over by wagons, drownings at river crossings, gunshots while loading firearms — killed many more. Hailstorms, lightning, blizzards in the Rockies and stampedes of oxen all took their toll. Of around 350,000 people who crossed the Plains by 1860, perhaps 20,000 died — roughly one in seventeen.

In 1846 a party of 87 California-bound migrants led by George Donner left the Oregon Trail to try a shortcut described in a guidebook by Lansford Hastings — a route Hastings himself had never travelled. The detour cost three weeks. The group reached the Sierra Nevada in late October, just as the first heavy snows hit the passes. Trapped at a high mountain lake (now called Donner Lake), 41 of the 87 died over the winter; some of the survivors ate the bodies of those who had died. The story horrified the East but did not stop the migration — if anything, it underlined the importance of leaving Independence early enough in the spring and trusting the established trail.

The 1848 Gold Strike

On 24 January 1848 a Connecticut carpenter named James Marshall, building a sawmill on the American River for the Swiss landowner John Sutter, spotted gold flakes in the river bed. The news leaked despite efforts to keep it quiet, and by the autumn it had reached the East. President Polk announced the discovery in his December 1848 message to Congress. In 1849 around 80,000 men — the original forty-niners — rushed to California by sea around Cape Horn, by the Panama route, or overland on the California Trail. Within two years California’s population had jumped from around 14,000 to over 220,000, and it was admitted to the Union as a state in 1850.

Boom Towns and Lawlessness

Mining camps grew into boom towns within months. San Francisco, a small port of 800 in 1848, had 25,000 inhabitants by 1850. Tents gave way to clapboard buildings and saloons; prices for food, tools and lodging soared because supplies could not keep up with demand. Most miners worked as individuals with pans and rockers along stream beds — placer mining — and few struck it rich. Far more money was made selling shovels, eggs and whisky than digging for gold.

Boom towns had no functioning legal system at first. With courts hundreds of miles away, miners formed vigilance committees to deal with theft and murder. The committees sometimes worked — San Francisco’s 1851 committee shut down a violent gang in days — and sometimes lynched the wrong man. The lawlessness fed wider stereotypes of the West that would last into the 20th century.

The Gold Rush transformed the West in ways the trickle of pioneer farmers had not. It pulled in roughly 25,000 Chinese immigrants between 1849 and 1854, who faced violence and discriminatory taxes. It tore up rivers and forests for hydraulic mining and timber. It pushed Native Californians off their land, and the state’s Native population fell from around 150,000 in 1845 to under 30,000 by 1870. And it accelerated calls for a transcontinental railroad — eventually built in 1869 — because the months-long sea route around Cape Horn was no longer fit for purpose.

Key Fact

The 1848 strike at Sutter’s Mill triggered the California Gold Rush. Around 80,000 forty-niners arrived in 1849 alone; California’s population grew fifteenfold by 1850; statehood followed the same year; and the rush sped up displacement of Native peoples and the call for a transcontinental railroad.

lessons.title: The Plains Indians' Way of Life

before.exam_tip_html: The 4-mark ‘Why interpretations differ’ question on this option often pairs a Turner-era view of the Plains as ‘empty’ or ‘primitive’ with a modern view that foregrounds Plains agency. Examiners flag a recurring confusion: students explain HOW the views differ (what each one says) when the question asks WHY (authors’ purpose, time of writing, evidence used). Top answers spend almost no words on what each interpretation says and almost all of them on why two writers would reach different verdicts — one writing in the 1890s with no Native sources, one writing today with tribal histories available.
before.content_html:
A Continent of Different Peoples

Students often write about ‘the Plains Indians’ or even ‘the Sioux’ as if every Native person between the Mississippi and the Rockies belonged to a single people. The reality is much richer. The Plains were home to dozens of nations, each with its own language, leadership and territory: the Lakota Sioux in the northern Plains, the Cheyenne and Arapaho on the central Plains, the Comanche on the southern Plains, the Crow in the Yellowstone country, the Pawnee on the Platte River. They sometimes allied with one another — and they sometimes fought one another fiercely. The Crow scouted FOR the US Army against the Lakota at Little Bighorn. Treating these nations as a single bloc misses how the unit’s wars actually unfolded.

Key Fact

The Plains were not a single ‘Indian’ world. Major nations included the Lakota Sioux, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Comanche, Crow and Pawnee. Each had its own language, territory and leadership, and the relationships between them were often hostile, not united.

The Horse and the Buffalo

Two animals shaped almost everything else. The Spanish had brought horses to the Americas in the 1500s; by 1750 horses had spread across the Plains, and Native peoples who had once hunted on foot became some of the finest horse-mounted hunters and warriors in the world. The Comanche in particular built an empire of horse breeders and raiders that the historian Pekka Hämäläinen has called ‘the dominant power of the southern Plains’. The second animal was the bison — the buffalo. An estimated 30–60 million buffalo roamed the Plains in 1840. Plains nations followed the herds, hunting them on horseback with bow and lance, and using almost every part of the carcass: meat for food, hide for clothes and tipi covers, sinew for thread, bones for tools, dung for fuel.

Because the buffalo moved with the seasons, settlement followed. The Plains nations lived in tipis — conical tents of buffalo hide on long poles. A skilled woman could take down a tipi in fifteen minutes and remount it on a horse-drawn travois. This portability was the secret of nomadic life: people did not move because they were unsettled; they moved because the buffalo did.

Bands, Tribes and Nations

Plains society was built in layers. A family belonged to a band — a group of perhaps 100 people who travelled together and hunted together. Several bands made up a tribe, sharing a language and customs. Several related tribes formed a nation, such as the Lakota or the Cheyenne. Decisions were made by councils of elders, not by a single all-powerful king. Chiefs were chosen for wisdom, generosity and bravery rather than birth, and they could be replaced. Below the chiefs were warrior societies, which policed the camp, organised hunts and led raids. White officials in Washington often did not understand this structure: they would press a single chief to sign a treaty and assume his signature bound every band, when no chief could speak for any band but his own.

Most Plains nations recognised a single spiritual presence behind nature, often translated in English as the Great Spirit or, in Lakota, Wakan Tanka. Earth was a living mother. Land was not owned but shared. Some places — such as the Black Hills of Dakota for the Lakota — were sacred and could never be sold. A young man would seek personal direction through a vision quest: alone on a hilltop, fasting for several days, he hoped for a vision that would guide his life and identify a personal animal protector. These beliefs would clash directly with US ideas of land as private property.

Warfare on the Plains

Plains warfare looked very different from European warfare and was often misread by white observers. Raids were small, fast and aimed at horses, captives or revenge rather than territory. Honour came not from killing but from counting coup — touching an enemy in battle without killing him — or from rescuing a fallen friend. A successful raid might kill nobody but bring home thirty horses and a story to tell. White officers often dismissed this as cowardice; in fact it was a different concept of bravery, one in which proximity to the enemy mattered more than body count.

Inter-tribal conflict was real and serious. The Lakota expanded into the Black Hills in the 1770s by pushing out the Cheyenne and Crow; the Comanche fought rivals across the southern Plains. By 1840, however, smallpox — spread by white settlers along the Missouri — had already killed perhaps half the population of the Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations. The Plains world the early settlers met was one already changed by European arrival.

Three contrasts stand out. First, land: Plains nations saw the earth as a shared mother; the United States ran on private title deeds. Second, government: Plains decisions were made by councils with limited authority; Washington negotiated as if a single chief could sign for all his people. Third, progress: 19th-century American culture treated farming, towns and ploughs as the definition of civilisation. Buffalo-hunting nomadism, no matter how successful, looked to settlers like a stage to be moved past. None of these gaps was easily bridged, and each helps explain why peace policies broke down so often.

Key Fact

The buffalo was the foundation of Plains life. Hide became tipi covers and clothing; meat became food (eaten fresh or dried as pemmican); sinew was used as thread; bones became tools and weapons; dung was burned as fuel where wood was scarce. To destroy the buffalo, as the US Army would later set out to do, was to destroy the way of life.

before.exam_tip_html: Period-study questions on this lesson often ask students to track change over time, and examiners punish chronologies that just list events. Top answers explain why each new policy was a response to the failure of the one before it. lessons.title: Fort Laramie 1851 and the Indian Wars 1862-1867

before.exam_tip_html: The 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation question is where this lesson’s detail pays off. Examiners reward answers that anchor evaluation in named events — Sand Creek, Fetterman, the 1868 Treaty — rather than generalising about ‘the Indian Wars’. If the interpretation calls Native defeat inevitable, name Red Cloud’s War as the counter-example: the only war in US history a Native nation won. Specific contextual knowledge is what lifts these answers into the top band.
before.content_html:
A Treaty That Looked Like Peace

By 1851 the United States was running into a problem on the central Plains. Pioneer wagon trains rolling along the Oregon and California Trails were stripping the Platte River valley of grass and game and bringing cholera into Native camps. Plains nations — especially the Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho — were responding with raids on the wagon trains. Washington wanted the trails open. The Plains nations wanted compensation and recognised territories. In September 1851, around 10,000 people from the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Shoshone, Mandan, Hidatsa and Arikara nations gathered at Horse Creek, near Fort Laramie in modern Wyoming, to negotiate.

The Fort Laramie Treaty assigned each nation a defined territory. The Lakota got land between the North Platte and the Missouri; the Cheyenne and Arapaho got the central Plains around the upper Arkansas; the Crow got the Yellowstone country. In return, the United States promised an annuity of $50,000 a year in goods for fifty years and a guarantee that wagon trains would not interfere with hunting. Both sides regarded the meeting as the largest peace conference yet held on the Plains.

Key Fact

The 1851 Fort Laramie Treaty assigned defined territories to the Lakota, Cheyenne, Arapaho, Crow, Shoshone and other Plains nations, in return for $50,000 a year in goods (later cut to ten years by the US Senate) and safe passage of wagon trains on the Oregon and California Trails.

Why Concentration Failed

Within a few years the treaty was unravelling. Four pressures explain why. First, the Senate quietly cut the annuity term from fifty years to ten without renegotiating with the signatories — a unilateral change Plains nations regarded as a broken promise. Second, no Plains nation was a single political body, so chiefs who had signed could not bind every band. Third, settler pressure on the Plains kept growing: the 1859 Pike’s Peak gold rush in Colorado triggered a flood of miners through the heart of Cheyenne and Arapaho land. Fourth, US officials decided to push the line further: the 1861 Treaty of Fort Wise stripped most of the central Plains land back from the Cheyenne and Arapaho, leaving them a small strip in eastern Colorado.

The Indian Wars Open: Dakota 1862

The cycle of war that defines this part of the unit began not on the Plains but in Minnesota. By summer 1862 annuity payments to the Dakota Sioux were months late, the harvest had failed, and a trader called Andrew Myrick had reportedly told a starving delegation, “Let them eat grass.” In August 1862 four young Dakota men killed five white settlers; their chief, Little Crow, reluctantly led a wider uprising in which roughly 600 settlers were killed. The army crushed the revolt within weeks. President Lincoln reviewed the resulting trials and sentenced 38 Dakota men to be hanged at Mankato on 26 December 1862 — the largest single-day mass execution in US history. The Dakota War showed that broken treaties plus settler pressure could quickly produce open war on the central Plains.

In autumn 1864 the Cheyenne peace chief Black Kettle had brought his band to camp near Sand Creek in eastern Colorado, flying a US flag and a white flag of truce after promises of safety from the local commander. At dawn on 29 November 1864 a force of around 700 Colorado militia under Colonel John Chivington attacked the camp. Around 150 Cheyenne and Arapaho were killed, the great majority women, children and the elderly; survivors testified that bodies were mutilated and trophies displayed in Denver theatres. Chivington called it a victory; a US Congressional inquiry called it “a foul and dastardly massacre” that had “disgraced the very name of an American soldier.” Sand Creek became the moment hopes of peaceful concentration died on the central Plains.

Fetterman’s Trap and Red Cloud’s War

In the north a second crisis was unfolding. The 1862 Bozeman Trail crossed straight through Lakota hunting grounds in modern Wyoming on its way to the Montana goldfields. The Lakota war leader Red Cloud warned that any new fort on the trail meant war. The army built three forts anyway. On 21 December 1866, near Fort Phil Kearny, a small detachment under Captain William Fetterman pursued a Lakota decoy party led by Crazy Horse over a ridge; behind the ridge waited 1,500–2,000 Lakota, Cheyenne and Arapaho warriors. All 81 men in Fetterman’s detachment were killed in less than an hour. Fetterman’s Trap was the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until Little Bighorn ten years later.

Two years of stalemate followed. Red Cloud’s warriors kept the forts under siege; the army could not safely use the trail. In 1868, in the second Fort Laramie Treaty, the United States agreed to abandon the three forts, close the Bozeman Trail, and recognise a Great Sioux Reservation including the sacred Black Hills of Dakota. Red Cloud’s War is the only war in US history that ended with a Native nation forcing the United States to give up land it had claimed.

Three consequences mattered for the rest of the period. First, trust between Plains nations and the federal government collapsed; even peace chiefs like Black Kettle (later killed at Washita in 1868) became symbols of broken promises. Second, the army on the Plains grew sharply: by 1869 it had 25,000 men permanently west of the Mississippi. Third, eastern public opinion split — the Sand Creek Congressional inquiry shocked many in the East, while frontier newspapers cheered Chivington. The 1868 Treaty looked like a Lakota victory but it locked Plains nations onto reservations whose boundaries would soon be redrawn.

Key Fact

Sand Creek (29 November 1864) destroyed Cheyenne trust in negotiation and prompted a Congressional inquiry. Fetterman’s Trap (21 December 1866) was the worst US Army defeat on the Plains until 1876 and forced the United States to abandon the Bozeman Trail forts in the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty.

lessons.title: North vs South: the Road to the Civil War

before.content_html:
Two Economies, One Country

By 1850 the United States looked like two countries pretending to be one. The North was industrialising fast: by 1860 it had 1.3 million factory workers, 70% of the country’s railway track and a free-labour culture in which workers could (in theory) save, leave a job and start their own business. The South was a plantation economy whose wealth came from cotton, sugar and tobacco grown by enslaved labour. Around 4 million people were held in slavery in the South in 1860, on the eve of war. The wealthiest 1,500 families on the Continent — the so-called planter class — held political power in southern state capitals and shaped southern politics in Washington.

Key Fact

By 1860 around 4 million people were held in slavery in the southern states, while the North held roughly 70% of the country’s railway track and 1.3 million factory workers. The two regions were not just politically different — their entire labour systems were incompatible.

The Real Quarrel: Slavery’s Expansion

A common student answer is that ‘the Civil War was about slavery’. The historiographical consensus is sharper. The proximate fight was not over slavery’s existence in the South — the federal government did not have the constitutional power to abolish it there — but over slavery’s expansion into new western territories. The 1820 Missouri Compromise had managed the issue for thirty years. It admitted Missouri as a slave state and Maine as a free state to keep the Senate balanced, and drew a line at latitude 36°30′ across the Louisiana Purchase: north of the line, no new slave states; south of it, slavery permitted.

The Mexican Cession of 1848 dropped a vast new territory into a country whose Compromise had been written for the Louisiana Purchase. The 1850 Compromise tried to patch the system: California entered as a free state, the Fugitive Slave Act required northerners to return runaway enslaved people, and the slave trade was banned in Washington DC. The patch held for four years. In 1854 Stephen Douglas’s Kansas-Nebraska Act repealed the Missouri Compromise altogether: in any new territory the question of slavery would now be decided by the votes of settlers themselves — popular sovereignty.

Bleeding Kansas and Dred Scott

The 1854 Act made Kansas the front line. Anti-slavery free-soilers and pro-slavery Missourians both rushed in to swing the vote. By 1856 the territory had two rival governments and open political violence: in May, pro-slavery raiders sacked the free-soil town of Lawrence; days later, the abolitionist John Brown led the killing of five pro-slavery settlers at Pottawatomie Creek. Eastern newspapers christened the territory ‘Bleeding Kansas’. In 1857 the Supreme Court ruled in Dred Scott v. Sandford that Black people could not be US citizens and that Congress had no power to ban slavery in any territory — in effect declaring the entire 1820 Compromise unconstitutional. Northern opinion was outraged.

Three currents of abolitionism shaped public opinion. Harriet Beecher Stowe’s 1852 novel Uncle Tom’s Cabin sold 300,000 copies in its first year and 1.5 million in Britain — Lincoln reportedly greeted Stowe in 1862 as “the little woman who wrote the book that made this great war”. The Underground Railroad, a network of safe houses and guides, helped perhaps 100,000 enslaved people escape to free states or Canada between 1810 and 1860; conductors like Harriet Tubman became national figures. And the abolitionist John Brown moved from Kansas to a far more dramatic act: in October 1859 he led a raid on the federal arsenal at Harpers Ferry, hoping to spark a slave uprising. Brown was captured and hanged within two months. To the South his raid proved that abolitionists meant insurrection; to many in the North he became a martyr.

Lincoln, Davis and the Election of 1860

By 1860 the political parties had broken along the same fault line. The Republican Party, founded in 1854, opposed slavery’s expansion (though not its existence in the South). Its candidate, Abraham Lincoln, ran on a platform of stopping slavery from spreading any further west. The Democratic Party split into northern and southern wings, fielding two candidates and dividing its vote. Lincoln won the November 1860 election with 40% of the popular vote and a comfortable majority in the Electoral College — without carrying a single southern state. Within six weeks South Carolina had voted to secede; by February 1861 seven states had formed the Confederate States of America with Jefferson Davis as president. Four more states joined after war began.

The trigger was Fort Sumter, a federal garrison in Charleston harbour, South Carolina. Lincoln refused to surrender it. Confederate forces opened fire on 12 April 1861. The fort fell within 36 hours and Lincoln called for 75,000 volunteers. The Civil War — the bloodiest in American history — had begun.

Examiners regularly flag a recurring student error on this option: writing ‘the war was about slavery’ and stopping there. The historiographical consensus, set out by James McPherson and others, is more precise: the proximate fight was over slavery’s expansion into new territories. Saying so explicitly — and showing why the Missouri Compromise, Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott decision and Lincoln’s 1860 platform all turned on that issue — is what separates a top-band answer from a competent one.

Key Fact

The path to civil war ran through four key dates: 1820 Missouri Compromise (managed slavery’s expansion); 1854 Kansas-Nebraska Act (repealed it); 1857 Dred Scott decision (struck the entire Compromise down); 1860 Lincoln election and 1861 Fort Sumter (turned political crisis into shooting war).
before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Period Essay on the causes of the Civil War, do not slip into the ‘the war was about slavery — full stop’ shortcut. Top-band answers say the war was about slavery’s expansion, then prove it: the Missouri Compromise, the Kansas-Nebraska Act, Dred Scott and Lincoln’s 1860 platform all turn on the question of new western territories. That precision is what examiner reports describe as the difference between a B- and an A-grade response.

lessons.title: The Civil War: Impact on Civilians

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Union naval blockade on civilians in the Confederate states between 1861 and 1865.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed effects, each supported by precise factual detail (specific shortages, prices, riots) and linked back to the question of civilian experience.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some supporting detail; clear focus on civilians.
Developing: One effect developed and one weak, or two effects covered superficially.
Emerging: Generalised description of the blockade with little focus on civilian impact.

Indicative content:
• Severe shortages of food, salt, medicine and imported goods, leading to malnutrition in Southern cities.
• Hyperinflation: Confederate dollars collapsed, with a barrel of flour reaching $1,000 by 1865.
• The Richmond Bread Riots of April 1863, in which mostly women looted shops in the Confederate capital.
• Disruption of cotton exports, undercutting plantation revenue and forcing planters to borrow heavily.
• Damage to civilian morale that contributed to desertion rates rising in the Confederate army from late 1863 onwards.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the Emancipation Proclamation of 1 January 1863 on civilians in the United States.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise detail and clear distinction between civilian groups (Black, white, Northern, Southern).
Secure: Two clear effects with some supporting detail.
Developing: One developed effect and one weak, or both partially covered.
Emerging: Vague comment on slavery without specific Proclamation effects.

Indicative content:
• Around 200,000 Black men joined the Union Army and Navy after January 1863, transforming the demographics of the Union forces.
• Hundreds of thousands of enslaved people fled to Union lines as ‘contraband’, weakening Southern plantation labour.
• Deepened opposition among some Northern Democrats, who saw the war shifting from Union preservation to abolition.
• Reframed the war internationally — Britain and France, both of which had abolished slavery, found it harder to recognise the Confederacy diplomatically.
• Did not free enslaved people in the loyal border states, leaving a legal gap that the 13th Amendment (1865) closed.

practice_questions.text:
‘The biggest impact of the American Civil War on civilians was economic.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider both the economic impact and other types of impact on civilians.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: A sustained argument that weighs economic impact against social, racial or political impact and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout; specialist vocabulary (Greenback, conscription, contraband, hyperinflation).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both sides of the statement, with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of economic and other impacts, but limited weighing or judgement.
Emerging: Description of the war’s effects with little engagement with the ‘biggest’ framing.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (economic was biggest):
• Confederate hyperinflation and collapse of currency.
• Northern industrial boom and the introduction of Greenbacks, income tax and national banks.
• Sherman’s March to the Sea destroyed an estimated $100 million of Southern economic infrastructure.
• Long-term: Southern agriculture took decades to recover; the North accelerated its industrial lead.
Challenging the statement:
• Social impact: 200,000 women entered the Northern workforce or nursing; gender roles shifted.
• Racial impact: emancipation, Black military service and the eventual 13th Amendment transformed the lives of around 4 million enslaved people.
• Political impact: vast expansion of federal power and a permanent shift in the federal-state balance.
• Human cost: 620,000 dead, ~2 per cent of the US population, leaving widows, orphans and disabled veterans across both sections.
Judgement: economic impact was profound but inseparable from racial and political change; a top-band answer reaches an explicit overall verdict and justifies it.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the New York Draft Riots of July 1863 on civilian society in the North.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual support; clearly distinguishes immediate from longer-term consequences.
Secure: Two clear effects with some development.
Developing: One effect developed; one weak or general.
Emerging: Description of the riots without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Exposed deep class tensions in Northern society — the $300 commutation fee was attacked as ‘a rich man’s war and a poor man’s fight’.
• At least 119 people killed; Black New Yorkers were targeted, with the Colored Orphan Asylum on Fifth Avenue burned down.
• Federal troops were diverted from Gettysburg battle aftermath to restore order, showing the war’s reach into Northern cities.
• Damaged Lincoln administration support among Irish-American communities.
• Forced the federal government to refine conscription, including buying out poorer draftees and prioritising volunteer recruitment for the rest of the war.

practice_questions.text:
‘Civilians in the South suffered far more than civilians in the North during the American Civil War.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider Southern civilian experience and Northern civilian experience.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; precise detail on both sections; deploys specialist vocabulary.
Secure: Clear comparison of Northern and Southern experience with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both sections but weighing limited; judgement implicit.
Emerging: Description of one section more than the other; little comparison.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (South suffered more):
• Naval blockade caused chronic shortages and starvation; bread riots in Richmond 1863.
• Hyperinflation made Confederate currency worthless by 1865.
• Sherman’s March physically destroyed Georgia and the Carolinas; cities such as Atlanta and Columbia burned.
• Around 25 per cent of military-age Southern white men died in the war; widows, orphans and disabled veterans concentrated in the South.
Challenging the statement:
• Northern conscription riots (NYC 1863) caused at least 119 deaths and exposed bitter class divisions.
• Northern food prices rose sharply, eroding wages.
• Around 360,000 Union soldiers died; their families were Northern civilians.
• Around 4 million enslaved people, mostly in the South, gained freedom — their wartime experience was suffering AND liberation, complicating any simple suffering league table.
Judgement: in absolute terms the South’s civilian collapse was deeper, but a top answer recognises that Black Southern civilians experienced something the North did not — emancipation — and weighs that into the judgement.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of Sherman’s March to the Sea (November–December 1864) on the civilian economy of the South.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise detail; engages with both physical and psychological dimensions.
Secure: Two clear effects, supported.
Developing: One developed effect and one general.
Emerging: Description of the march itself with little focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Direct destruction of an estimated $100 million of property — railroads (‘Sherman’s neckties’), mills, plantations, livestock.
• Disabled the Confederate transport network — supplies could no longer move from Georgia to Lee’s army in Virginia.
• Spread civilian fear: Sherman’s explicit aim to make Southerners ‘feel the hard hand of war’ broke confidence in Confederate ability to protect civilians.
• Accelerated desertion in the Confederate army as soldiers received letters describing destruction at home.
• Long-term: Georgia’s recovery into the 1880s was hampered by the loss of rail and agricultural infrastructure.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Explain Effects question on the war’s civilian impact, examiners reward answers that split the impact into clear strands — social and economic, North and South — rather than a single chronology of battles. Aim for two developed effects, each with a precise example (e.g. ‘the New York Draft Riots of July 1863 killed at least 119 people, showing how conscription split Northern society along class lines’). The 12-mark Period Essay rewards a substantiated overall judgement: was the war’s biggest civilian impact economic, social or political?
before.content_html:
A War of Civilians, Not Just Soldiers

The American Civil War of 1861–1865 cost roughly 620,000 soldiers’ lives, more than every other US war combined until Vietnam. But the spec is not interested in battles for their own sake — it asks about the social and economic impact on civilian populations. Northerners and Southerners experienced the war so differently that it is best understood as two separate home fronts running in parallel: one industrialising, one collapsing.

Key Fact

The American Civil War ran from April 1861 (Confederate attack on Fort Sumter) to April 1865 (Lee’s surrender at Appomattox). Around 620,000 soldiers died, more than 2 per cent of the US population — equivalent today to roughly 7 million American deaths.

The Northern Home Front: Boom Under Pressure

For the Union the war was an industrial accelerant. Northern factories, already growing before 1861, expanded sharply to supply uniforms, weapons, ammunition and railway track. Wages rose, although food prices rose faster. Women moved into factory and clerical work in unprecedented numbers, with around 200,000 entering the federal civil service or wartime nursing. Treasury Secretary Salmon Chase printed paper money — the Greenback — to fund the war effort, and Congress passed the first federal income tax in 1861.

Conscription arrived in March 1863 and proved bitterly unpopular. A wealthy man could pay $300 to avoid service or hire a substitute, which working-class men saw as proof of a ‘rich man’s war and a poor man’s fight’. The result was the New York Draft Riots of July 1863: four days of violence in which Irish-American workers attacked recruiting stations, federal buildings and Black New Yorkers. At least 119 people were killed before Union troops, fresh from Gettysburg, restored order.

The Southern Home Front: Collapse

The Confederacy faced the opposite trajectory. The Union naval blockade, declared by Lincoln in April 1861, choked off Southern cotton exports and the imported goods on which the South depended. Food shortages set in by 1862. Bread riots broke out in Richmond, Virginia in April 1863 when crowds of women looted shops. Confederate currency lost its value; by war’s end a barrel of flour cost $1,000 in Confederate dollars. Slave labour kept plantations running, but as Union armies advanced, hundreds of thousands of enslaved people walked off and crossed into Union lines as contraband.

From November to December 1864, Union General William Tecumseh Sherman led 60,000 troops on a 285-mile destructive march from Atlanta to Savannah, Georgia. His ‘total war’ strategy targeted the civilian economy — railroads were torn up and twisted into ‘Sherman’s neckties’, plantations burned, livestock taken or killed. Sherman estimated his march did $100 million of damage. The aim was to break Confederate civilian morale by showing the war could no longer be kept at arm’s length, and historians widely agree it shortened the war by months.

Slavery in Wartime

Lincoln did not begin the war as an abolitionist. His public goal in 1861 was to preserve the Union; he believed an immediate emancipation would push the border states (Maryland, Kentucky, Missouri) into the Confederacy. After the bloody Union victory at Antietam (September 1862), he moved. The Emancipation Proclamation, issued on 1 January 1863, declared all enslaved people in Confederate-held territory free. It did not legally free people in the Union border states, but it transformed the war’s meaning: the Union army was now an army of liberation.

Around 200,000 Black soldiers served in the Union Army and Navy from 1863, organised into the United States Coloured Troops. They were initially paid less than white soldiers and faced execution rather than capture if taken by Confederate forces. The famous 54th Massachusetts Regiment’s assault on Fort Wagner in July 1863 helped break Northern doubts that Black soldiers would fight.

Wartime emergency produced a permanent expansion of federal power. The 1861 Revenue Act introduced the first income tax. The 1862 Legal Tender Act made Greenbacks legal currency. The 1863 National Banking Act created federally chartered banks issuing a uniform currency — ending decades of state-bank chaos. The Homestead Act and Pacific Railroad Act, both 1862, channelled federal land into settlement and rail. The Republicans, in control of Congress while the Southern Democrats were absent, used the war to remake the American state.

Why the Sequence of Battles Matters Briefly

For civilians, three turning points mattered. Antietam (September 1862) was bloody but inconclusive militarily; politically it gave Lincoln the Union victory he needed to issue emancipation. Gettysburg and Vicksburg (both July 1863) broke the Confederacy’s strategic position — Gettysburg ended Lee’s last invasion of the North; Vicksburg gave the Union control of the Mississippi River, splitting the Confederacy in two. By spring 1865, with Atlanta fallen and Sherman in the Carolinas, Lee surrendered to Grant at Appomattox Court House on 9 April 1865. Lincoln was assassinated five days later by Confederate sympathiser John Wilkes Booth.

Key Fact

The Northern home front saw industrial growth, women in new jobs, paper currency and draft riots. The Southern home front saw blockade, hyperinflation, food riots and Sherman’s scorched-earth march. Both sides experienced massive expansion of federal power and the legal end of slavery in Confederate territory.

lessons.title: Mountain Meadows and the Mormon Question

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1962 history of the American West written for a general American readership):
‘The Mountain Meadows Massacre was the desperate act of a frontier community under siege. With Buchanan’s army marching towards them, the southern Utah Mormons believed any wagon train might carry hostile spies. The killings were a tragedy, but they were the work of frightened men in extraordinary circumstances, not a planned atrocity.’

Interpretation B (from a 2002 study by historians using newly released Latter-day Saint Church archives):
‘Mountain Meadows was not a panicked overreaction but a co-ordinated militia operation. Local leaders gave specific orders, the truce flag was a deliberate trap, and the cover-up that blamed the Paiute alone lasted twenty years. The massacre exposes the closed authority of the early Utah theocracy.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation B. In your answer you should refer to Interpretation A and use your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s argument; engages directly with the specific claims (co-ordinated, truce as trap, twenty-year cover-up, closed theocracy); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation of B with reference to A; some own knowledge applied; judgement reached.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to summarise rather than weigh; one or two pieces of own knowledge.
Emerging: Describes the interpretations or the topic without evaluating B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Truce flag tactic and direct involvement of John D. Lee — planning, not panic.
• The cover-up blaming the Paiute alone held for almost two decades.
• Lee’s 1876 trial revealed militia structure and chain of command.
• Federal investigators were obstructed for years by Mormon authorities.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• The Utah War of 1857–58 created genuine fears of federal invasion.
• Local rumours linked the Arkansas party to anti-Mormon violence in Missouri.
• Most modern Mormon scholarship rejects the ‘direct order from Brigham Young’ thesis.

Judgement: B is the stronger explanation of how the killings happened, but a top-band answer notes that A captures the war-hysteria context that made militia action thinkable in the first place.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B again.

Interpretation A: 1962 history of the American West written for a general American readership.
Interpretation B: 2002 study by historians using newly released Latter-day Saint Church archives.

Suggest reasons why Interpretations A and B may differ in their views of the Mountain Meadows Massacre.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author purpose, evidence available, time of writing or audience — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons; some clarity.
Developing: One reason developed and one weak; or both partially explained.
Emerging: Reasons describe what each interpretation says, missing the question.

Indicative content:
• Different evidence available: B uses Latter-day Saint Church archives released in the late 20th century, which the 1962 author of A could not see.
• Different time of writing: A was written in 1962, when American historiography was less revisionist; B in 2002, after the rise of revisionist Western history (Limerick, White) reframed frontier violence.
• Different purpose: A’s general-reader survey aimed for a digestible ‘tragedy’ framing; B’s academic study aimed to test responsibility precisely.
• Different audiences: A was written for a wide American readership in the early 1960s; B for an academic and Mormon-history audience post-millennium.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2010 study of US religious freedom):
‘Federal anti-polygamy laws between 1862 and 1890 were necessary defences of the rule of law. The Constitution could not tolerate a single religious group claiming the right to ignore federal statutes. The 1890 Manifesto was not a tragedy — it was the price of citizenship, and the Mormons paid it because they wanted to be Americans.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation C.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s argument; weighs the ‘necessary defence of law’ framing against alternative readings; supports judgement with precise own knowledge of the three federal laws and the 1890 Manifesto.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial use of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the laws without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• The Constitution required equal application of federal law in all territories.
• Plural marriage was widely judged exploitative of women in 19th-century debate.
• Mormons themselves accepted the 1890 Manifesto as the route to statehood — a form of consent.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• The 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act dissolved the Church and seized property — a level of state action against a religion unique in US history.
• Polygamy continued unofficially in some communities for years after 1890.
• An alternative reading sees the laws as religious coercion rather than constitutional defence.

Judgement: C captures one valid framing — constitutional defence — but a top-band response notes the laws went well beyond preventing polygamous unions to dismantling the Church itself.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C again.

Interpretation C: a 2010 study of US religious freedom.
Interpretation D (from a 1998 social history written by a Latter-day Saint historian):
‘The Edmunds-Tucker Act of 1887 was an act of religious persecution. The dissolution of the Church and the confiscation of its property went far beyond punishing polygamy. The 1890 Manifesto was a forced surrender, made under economic and legal duress, by a community whose alternative was destruction.’

Suggest reasons why Interpretations C and D may differ in their views of the federal anti-polygamy laws.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons focused on author identity/purpose, audience, evidence emphasis or framing — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed reason and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons summarise the interpretations rather than explaining difference.

Indicative content:
• Different author standpoints: C is written from a constitutional/legal-history perspective; D by a Mormon historian using community sources and oral memory.
• Different evidence emphasis: C focuses on statutes and federal-court reasoning; D on the lived experience of Mormon families under prosecution.
• Different purpose: C aims to defend a constitutional principle; D aims to recover a community story of suffering.
• Different audiences: C addresses a legal-academic readership; D writes within and for a Latter-day Saint scholarly community.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1995 academic study of US territorial expansion):
‘The fundamental obstacle to Utah statehood was not polygamy at all but theocracy. Washington could not accept a community where civic and religious authority were the same person. The 1890 Manifesto only became a route to statehood because it implied the separation of church and state Brigham Young had refused.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation E.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘theocracy not polygamy’ thesis; substantiates judgement with precise own knowledge of Mormon-federal relations 1857–1896.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial use of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with E’s specific argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Buchanan sent the 1857 army against Mormon political control, not solely against polygamy.
• The Edmunds Act stripped Mormons of voting rights in Utah — an attack on theocratic governance.
• Federally appointed governors and judges were specifically designed to break Mormon civic dominance.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Public Eastern outrage was framed primarily around polygamy, not theocracy.
• The 1882 and 1887 Acts targeted plural marriage by name.
• The 1890 Manifesto explicitly addressed marriage practice, not church-state separation.

Judgement: E offers a sharp insight — theocratic authority WAS as alarming to Washington as plural marriage — but a top-band answer recognises both targets shaped federal action.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E again.

Interpretation E: a 1995 academic study of US territorial expansion.
Interpretation F (from a popular history of the American West, published 2018):
‘The Mormon question was settled by money. The 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act seized Church property and pushed the Latter-day Saints towards bankruptcy. Once survival was at stake, plural marriage became negotiable in a way it had never been when only principle was on the table.’

Suggest reasons why Interpretations E and F may differ in their views of how the Mormon question was settled.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in audience, purpose, evidence and time of writing — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe interpretations rather than explaining difference.

Indicative content:
• Different audiences and purposes: E is an academic territorial-expansion study foregrounding constitutional theory; F is a popular history foregrounding pragmatic and economic causes that engage general readers.
• Different evidence emphasis: E focuses on the apparatus of governance (governors, voting rights); F on Church finances and the property seizure.
• Different historiographical framing: E sits in 1990s political history; F in 2010s revisionist popular history with a more cynical view of religious-political compromise.
• Different time of writing: F (2018) follows decades of work emphasising material and economic factors in religious history.
