Test the claim against precise evidence (Mountain Meadows, John D. Lee’s execution, the three anti-polygamy laws, the 1890 Manifesto), and weigh the parts of the interpretation you accept against the parts you would qualify. For 4-mark ‘Why Interpretations Differ’, focus on author purpose, evidence used and time of writing — not on what each interpretation actually says.
before.content_html:
A Religious Refuge Inside an Expanding Empire

When Brigham Young led the Mormons into the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, he intended to build Deseret — a self-governing religious community far enough from the United States to escape persecution. Within a year the Mexican-American War had brought the same valley inside US territory. The story of the Mormon question between 1847 and 1896 is the story of how Washington reluctantly accepted, then forced, this religious community to become a regular American state.

Key Fact

The Mormons were founded by Joseph Smith in upstate New York in 1830. After persecution and Smith’s murder in Illinois in 1844, Brigham Young led the surviving community to the Salt Lake Valley in 1847, then part of Mexico. The 1848 Treaty of Guadalupe Hidalgo placed it inside the United States.

The Utah War, 1857–58

By the mid-1850s federal officials sent to Utah were complaining that Brigham Young’s theocracy had no respect for outside law. Polygamy — the Mormon practice of plural marriage — had been publicly admitted in 1852 and outraged Eastern opinion. President James Buchanan responded in 1857 by sending an army of 2,500 federal troops under Albert Sidney Johnston to install a non-Mormon governor and assert federal authority. Mormon militia harassed the supply trains, burning forts and stampeding cattle but avoiding direct battle. The standoff — later called the Utah War — ended in 1858 with Young accepting a federal governor while remaining the community’s real leader.

The Mountain Meadows Massacre, September 1857

In the middle of this paranoid summer, on 11 September 1857, around 50 men from a southern Utah Mormon militia, joined by some local Paiute men they had recruited, attacked the Baker-Fancher wagon train — a party of around 140 emigrants from Arkansas heading for California. After a five-day siege, the militia approached the wagon train under a flag of truce, promising safe escort. They then turned on the unarmed party and killed about 120 men, women and older children. Only seventeen children, all under seven, were spared.

The motives were a tangle: war hysteria over the approaching federal army, suspicions that the Arkansas party was somehow connected to the killing of a Mormon apostle in Missouri years earlier, plain greed for the wagon train’s livestock and goods, and the encouragement of local Mormon militia leader John D. Lee. After the killings the militiamen swore a written oath of secrecy, and the southern Utah leadership tried to blame the entire massacre on Paiute warriors alone — a cover-up that held for almost twenty years and shielded most of the Mormon militia from prosecution.

Federal investigators reopened the case after the Civil War. John D. Lee was tried twice; his second trial, in 1876, ended in conviction and his execution by firing squad at the massacre site itself in March 1877. Lee was the only person ever executed for the killings, and many at the time and since have argued he was made the scapegoat for a wider Mormon militia leadership. Brigham Young died in 1877, six months after Lee’s execution; his exact role in ordering or authorising the killings remains contested by historians today.

Federal Anti-Polygamy Laws

Mormon-federal relations stayed tense for decades after the war. Congress targeted polygamy with three escalating laws. The 1862 Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act made plural marriage illegal in US territories but went largely unenforced because of the Civil War. The 1882 Edmunds Act made polygamy a felony, disqualified polygamists from voting and holding office, and removed Mormon control of Utah’s electoral machinery. Tensions peaked when the 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act dissolved the Latter-day Saint Church as a legal corporation and confiscated much of its property.

Faced with this assault on the Church’s survival, Mormon president Wilford Woodruff issued the 1890 Manifesto ending the Church’s official sanction of new plural marriages. With polygamy formally renounced, Congress agreed to admit Utah as the 45th state in January 1896, almost half a century after Brigham Young first reached the valley.

The Mormon question matters because it shows the United States wrestling with religious diversity inside its expanding empire. Federal policy treated plural marriage as a threat to the family and to the rule of law — the same federal state that crushed the Confederacy and corralled Native nations onto reservations also forced the Mormons to abandon a defining religious practice as the price of full citizenship. Different historians frame this story differently: some see federal action as a defence of constitutional law and women’s welfare, while others see it as religious coercion and the suppression of an alternative American community.

Key Fact

The federal-Mormon settlement was forced by three escalating laws: the 1862 Morrill Anti-Bigamy Act, the 1882 Edmunds Act and the 1887 Edmunds-Tucker Act. The 1890 Mormon Manifesto ended the Church’s sanction of new plural marriages, opening the path to Utah statehood in 1896.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1929 US history textbook):
‘Reconstruction was a tragic era. Carpetbaggers and ignorant freedmen, propped up by federal bayonets, plundered the prostrate South. The white people of the South suffered as no Americans had ever suffered before, until at last decent citizens reasserted control in 1877.’

Interpretation B (from a 1988 academic study of Reconstruction):
‘Reconstruction was an unfinished revolution. Around 2,000 Black men held public office, the first state-funded schools were built across the South, and three constitutional amendments redefined American citizenship. The tragedy was not Black participation but its violent overthrow.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation B. In your answer you should refer to Interpretation A and use your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s ‘unfinished revolution’ thesis; engages directly with its specific claims (2,000 Black officials, schools, amendments, violent overthrow); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation of B with reference to A; relevant own knowledge; judgement reached.
Developing: Some evaluation but tends to summarise; one or two pieces of own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without evaluating B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Hiram Revels (Mississippi, 1870) and around 16 Black Congressmen show genuine political participation.
• The Freedmen’s Bureau founded around 4,000 schools and distributed 21 million rations.
• The 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments rewrote constitutional citizenship.
• Reconstruction state governments funded the South’s first public-education systems.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• ‘Forty acres and a mule’ was rescinded; freedpeople did not gain economic independence.
• Sharecropping replaced slavery as a coercive labour system.
• Some state legislatures did experience corruption (Louisiana, South Carolina).
• Reconstruction was overthrown by violence rather than collapsing of its own weight.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes that A captures the post-1877 narrative deliberately built to discredit Reconstruction.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 1965 popular history of post-war America):
‘The 13th Amendment ended slavery in name but the Black Codes recreated it in substance. Mississippi led the way: vagrancy laws criminalised unemployment, apprenticeship laws bound Black children to white employers, and contracts forced workers to sign for a year or face arrest. Without the 14th Amendment and the 1866 Civil Rights Act, freedom would have meant nothing.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation C.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s argument; engages with the specific claims about Black Codes recreating slavery and the role of federal action; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• Mississippi’s 1865 Black Code did include vagrancy, apprenticeship and contract clauses functioning as a substitute for slavery.
• Northern outrage at the Codes drove the 1866 Civil Rights Act and the 14th Amendment.
• Without federal intervention the codes would have remained on the books.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• ‘Recreated it in substance’ overstates — freedpeople could marry legally, hold property and could not be sold.
• The Freedmen’s Bureau provided real legal protection that slaves had never had.
• Black political participation under Radical Reconstruction goes beyond the framework C implies.

Judgement: C captures the threat the Codes posed and the necessity of federal action, but a top-band answer recognises that the new federal protections produced rights distinctly different from those available under slavery.

practice_questions.text:
‘Reconstruction was a successful experiment in multiracial democracy between 1865 and 1877.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider what was achieved and what was not.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs achievements against limits and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support throughout; deploys specialist vocabulary (freedman, Black Code, sharecropping, Radical Republican, Reconstruction Amendment).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant supporting detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Some discussion of both sides; limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of Reconstruction with little engagement with the ‘successful experiment’ framing.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (Reconstruction was a success):
• 13th, 14th and 15th Amendments redefined US citizenship.
• Around 2,000 Black officials elected, including Hiram Revels as first Black US Senator (1870).
• Around 4,000 schools founded by the Freedmen’s Bureau.
• 1866 Civil Rights Act — first federal civil rights law in US history.
• State-funded education systems established in many Southern states for the first time.

Challenging the statement:
• ‘Forty acres and a mule’ rescinded; sharecropping trapped freedpeople in debt.
• Black Codes reasserted control until federal intervention; even then, voter intimidation rose.
• Reconstruction was overthrown by 1877; rights granted on paper were violated in daily life.
• Andrew Johnson’s obstruction slowed reform; even Radical Reconstruction relied on federal troops who would soon withdraw.

Judgement: Reconstruction achieved more than the ‘tragic era’ framing allowed but less than its constitutional ambitions promised; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict and substantiates it.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation D.

Interpretation D (from a 1990 study of US constitutional history):
‘The 14th Amendment was the most important law passed in 19th-century America. It made citizenship national rather than state, guaranteed due process and equal protection, and gave the federal government the authority to defend individual rights against the states. Every later civil rights victory rested on it.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation D.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of D’s ‘most important law’ claim; weighs against alternatives (13th Amendment, 1866 Civil Rights Act, 15th Amendment); supports judgement with own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the 14th Amendment without engagement with D’s claim.

Indicative content (supporting D):
• Defined citizenship by birth on US soil — settling decades of debate.
• Created the Equal Protection and Due Process Clauses still central to US law.
• Provided the constitutional basis for later civil rights legislation.
• Federalised individual rights against state interference.

Indicative content (qualifying D):
• The 13th Amendment ended slavery itself — arguably more transformative.
• The 1866 Civil Rights Act preceded the 14th and provided its template.
• Practical enforcement of the 14th was weak in the 19th century — Plessy v. Ferguson (1896) hollowed out equal protection.
• Impact only became central in the 20th-century civil rights movement, decades after the Reconstruction era.

Judgement: D’s claim is defensible for long-term significance, but a top-band answer notes that the 14th’s 19th-century reach was limited by judicial retreat — the ‘most important law’ framing is a long-view verdict, not an 1868 one.

practice_questions.text:
‘The 13th Amendment was more important than the Civil Rights Act of 1866 in transforming the lives of formerly enslaved people.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider what each measure did.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; deploys specialist vocabulary; precise on both measures.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (13th was more important):
• Abolished slavery itself — the foundational change without which nothing else mattered.
• Constitutional, not statutory — harder to repeal.
• Applied uniformly across all states, including the loyal border states the Emancipation Proclamation had not reached.

Challenging the statement (Civil Rights Act mattered more in everyday life):
• Defined citizenship and equal rights to make contracts, sue, give evidence and own property.
• Gave federal courts jurisdiction over violations of these rights, providing a real remedy.
• Without it, Black Codes would have left freedom theoretical.
• Provided the legal template that became the 14th Amendment.

Judgement: the 13th was the more transformative single change in legal status; the 1866 Act made that change practically meaningful in daily Southern life. A top answer reaches a clear verdict on the comparison.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1995 social history of the post-war South):
‘The Freedmen’s Bureau was the most important federal agency of Reconstruction. Its schools educated a generation of Black children. Its courts protected freedpeople against fraudulent labour contracts. Its rations kept people alive in a war-shattered region. When it was wound down in 1872, much of the support structure for emancipation went with it.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation E.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s claim about the Bureau’s importance; weighs against alternatives (Constitutional Amendments, Civil Rights Act, military Reconstruction); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Bureau without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Around 4,000 schools founded; many of the South’s historically Black colleges began under Bureau auspices.
• 21 million rations distributed in the famine-stricken war zone.
• Bureau courts adjudicated thousands of labour-contract disputes in favour of freedpeople.
• Wind-down in 1872 coincided with the visible weakening of Reconstruction.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• The Bureau was always under-funded and under-staffed for the size of the South.
• Constitutional Amendments and the 1866 Civil Rights Act provided the deeper legal framework.
• Radical Reconstruction’s federal troops mattered as much as Bureau staff for protection.
• Bureau wind-down was a symptom rather than the cause of federal retreat.

Judgement: E captures the everyday significance of the Bureau but overstates its position in the wider architecture of Reconstruction; a top answer balances on-the-ground reach against constitutional reform.

before.content_html:
A Murder Reshapes Reconstruction

On the evening of 14 April 1865 — five days after Lee’s surrender at Appomattox — John Wilkes Booth shot Abraham Lincoln at Ford’s Theatre in Washington. Lincoln died the next morning. Reconstruction, the project of rebuilding the defeated South and integrating around 4 million formerly enslaved people into American life, suddenly fell to Vice President Andrew Johnson, a Tennessee Democrat with very different priorities to Lincoln. The next twelve years would see remarkable legal gains for Black Americans — and an equally remarkable rolling back.

Key Fact

The three Reconstruction Amendments transformed the US Constitution. The 13th (1865) abolished slavery; the 14th (1868) granted citizenship and equal protection to all people born in the US; the 15th (1870) banned the denial of voting rights on grounds of race. Together they redefined American citizenship.

Presidential Reconstruction, 1865–1866

Andrew Johnson believed the Southern states should rejoin the Union quickly and on lenient terms. His Presidential Reconstruction allowed each former Confederate state to write a new constitution, ratify the 13th Amendment and rejoin Congress with little intrusion. By the end of 1865 the 13th Amendment had been ratified and slavery was officially over — a constitutional revolution that fulfilled Lincoln’s war aim.

Within months, however, Southern state legislatures — many filled with former Confederates — passed laws known as Black Codes. These restricted formerly enslaved people’s ability to move, change jobs, own property in towns or testify in court against white men. Mississippi’s Code required Black workers to sign yearly labour contracts; vagrancy laws criminalised joblessness, allowing courts to lease Black defendants to white employers. Northerners watched the South recreating slavery under another name.

The 1866 Civil Rights Act and the Freedmen’s Bureau

Congress responded. The 1866 Civil Rights Act — passed over Johnson’s veto — declared that all persons born in the United States were citizens, with equal rights to make contracts, sue, give evidence and own property. It was the first federal civil rights law in US history. Alongside it, the Freedmen’s Bureau, established in March 1865 and renewed in 1866, distributed 21 million rations, founded around 4,000 schools, and supervised labour contracts and court cases for newly emancipated Southerners.

The 1866 mid-term elections gave Republicans a two-thirds majority in Congress, allowing them to override Johnson’s vetoes at will. The 1867 Reconstruction Acts divided the South into five military districts, suspended the existing state governments, and required new state constitutions guaranteeing Black male suffrage before any state could rejoin the Union. Federally appointed military governors enforced the law. Johnson’s attempts to obstruct led to his impeachment in 1868 — he survived removal from office by a single Senate vote.

Black Political Participation

Under Radical Reconstruction, Black Americans entered politics on a scale never seen before. Around 2,000 African Americans were elected to public office between 1867 and 1877, including 16 to the US Congress and around 600 to state legislatures. Hiram Revels became the first Black US Senator in 1870, taking the seat once held by Jefferson Davis. Frederick Douglass, the most prominent Black abolitionist, advocated tirelessly for Black suffrage and was eventually appointed US Marshal for Washington DC.

Reconstruction state governments expanded public education, building thousands of new schools (often the first in their districts for either race), invested in hospitals and railroads, and rewrote tax codes to fund the new spending. Many of these reforms outlasted Reconstruction and reshaped the South for generations.

Reform was real, but partial. The promise of ‘forty acres and a mule’ — redistributed land from former plantations — was rescinded by Johnson in 1865. Most freedpeople ended up as sharecroppers, working land owned by former slaveholders for a share of the crop. Debt and crop failure trapped many in poverty for the rest of their lives. Voting rights existed in law but were already being undermined by white-supremacist violence and intimidation by the late 1860s. Federal will was strong in 1867 but began ebbing within a decade.

From ‘Tragic Era’ to ‘Unfinished Revolution’

For most of the early 20th century, US textbooks called Reconstruction ‘the tragic era’ — a story of Northern occupation, corrupt government and victimised white Southerners. From the 1960s onwards historians, especially Eric Foner in his 1988 study Reconstruction: America’s Unfinished Revolution, reframed the period as a genuinely radical experiment in multiracial democracy that achieved real reforms before being broken by terror and federal retreat. This reframing is now the mainstream view and shapes how examiners reward top-band answers.

Key Fact

By 1870 Reconstruction had abolished slavery, granted citizenship and Black male suffrage, founded around 4,000 schools, and elected the first Black US Senator. But it had also failed to redistribute land, allowed Black Codes to be replaced by sharecropping, and was already meeting violent resistance from groups such as the Ku Klux Klan.

lessons.title: Carpetbaggers, the Klan and the End of Reconstruction

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1915 popular history written by a Southern Democrat):
‘The carpetbaggers were the great evil of the post-war South. They came down with empty pockets and left with full ones, leaving behind crushing taxes, broken state finances and the secret society of the Klan, which honourable Southerners formed in self-defence.’

Interpretation B (from a 1989 academic study of Reconstruction):
‘The carpetbagger stereotype is myth. Most Northerners who moved South were teachers, ministers, professionals and Union veterans. The Ku Klux Klan was founded in 1866 by Confederate veterans, not by carpetbaggers, and existed to attack the very people the Southern Democrat label sought to discredit.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation B. In your answer you should refer to Interpretation A and use your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s argument; engages with the specific claims (myth, professional carpetbaggers, Klan founded by Confederate veterans); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with reference to A; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the labels without engaging with B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Foner and Powell’s research shows around 50,000 Northerners moved South; many were teachers, lawyers and Union veterans.
• The Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, by six Confederate veterans in 1866; Nathan Bedford Forrest, a Confederate general, became its first Grand Wizard.
• Klan violence targeted carpetbaggers, scalawags and Black Republicans — the Klan attacked carpetbaggers, it did not include them.
• A minority of carpetbaggers were corrupt, but corruption existed across all post-war state governments, North and South.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• Some Reconstruction state governments did experience high taxes and corruption (Louisiana, South Carolina).
• A few high-profile carpetbagger administrators became personally wealthy — the stereotype had a kernel of evidence.
• The pre-1960s historiography that A reflects was the dominant US view for half a century.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes A reflects the post-1877 narrative built to discredit Reconstruction.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B again.

Interpretation A: 1915 popular history written by a Southern Democrat.
Interpretation B: 1989 academic study of Reconstruction.

Suggest reasons why Interpretations A and B may differ in their views of carpetbaggers.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author purpose, evidence available, time of writing or audience — not on what each interpretation says.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe what each interpretation says.

Indicative content:
• Different author standpoints: A is written by a Southern Democrat in 1915 with a partisan stake in the Reconstruction story; B is by an academic in 1989 with no comparable political loyalty.
• Different time of writing: A sits inside the ‘Lost Cause’ tradition dominant in early-20th-century Southern history; B follows the post-1960s revisionist turn led by Foner.
• Different evidence available: B can draw on local archives, military records and Bureau correspondence opened up later; A relies heavily on contemporary Southern Democrat polemic.
• Different audiences: A addresses a popular Southern readership comfortable with the ‘tragic era’ framing; B writes for an academic readership expecting evidence-led scholarship.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2003 study of US violence and law):
‘The Ku Klux Klan was destroyed by federal action between 1870 and 1872. The Enforcement Acts gave Grant the tools, the South Carolina prosecutions of 1871 used them, and within two years the original Klan had ceased to exist as a coherent national organisation. The story of how white-supremacist violence then continued belongs to the White Leagues, the Red Shirts and the Klan’s second incarnation in 1915.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation C.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s ‘destroyed by federal action’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Enforcement Acts, South Carolina prosecutions, successor groups); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Klan without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• The 1870 and 1871 Enforcement Acts criminalised interference with Black voting rights and authorised federal troops.
• Grant used the Klan Act in nine South Carolina counties in 1871; hundreds of Klansmen were prosecuted.
• The original Klan was effectively dispersed by 1872.
• White-supremacist violence reorganised under different names — White Leagues, Red Shirts — rather than continuing as the Klan.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• ‘Destroyed’ overstates — the rituals, hoods and ideology survived locally.
• Federal effort was uneven by region; rural Mississippi saw fewer prosecutions.
• White-supremacist violence in real continuity with the Klan continued throughout the 1870s under the new labels.
• The Klan’s 1915 revival drew on uninterrupted Southern memory.

Judgement: C captures a real federal achievement — the original Klan was broken — but a top-band answer notes that the underlying violence was not destroyed, only relabelled.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C again.

Interpretation C: a 2003 study of US violence and law.
Interpretation D (from a 1992 social history of African Americans in the South):
‘The Klan was never really destroyed in 1872. The men, the methods and the message all reappeared in the White Leagues and the Red Shirts within months. To call this a victory for federal law is to mistake a name change for a defeat.’

Suggest reasons why Interpretations C and D may differ in their views of how the Klan ended.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly distinct reasons rooted in author standpoint, evidence emphasis, audience or time of writing.
Secure: Two valid reasons.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Reasons describe interpretations.

Indicative content:
• Different evidence emphasis: C focuses on federal-law records and prosecutions; D on Black community memory and oral histories of continued terror.
• Different author standpoints: C is institutional/legal history; D is bottom-up social history of African American experience.
• Different audiences: C writes for a legal-history readership; D for a community-history readership.
• Different framings of success: C measures by organisational defeat of the Klan as a label; D by lived experience of ongoing white-supremacist violence.

practice_questions.text:
‘The Compromise of 1877 was the main reason Reconstruction ended.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider the Compromise of 1877 and other reasons.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Compromise against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (carpetbagger, scalawag, Redeemer, Enforcement Acts, Slaughter-House Cases).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of multiple causes with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of 1877 without engaging with the ‘main reason’ framing.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (Compromise was the main reason):
• The Compromise withdrew the last federal troops from the South in 1877.
• Without federal protection, Reconstruction state governments could not survive against organised intimidation.
• Hayes ratified what was already being negotiated locally between Northern and Southern Republicans.

Challenging the statement (other factors mattered more):
• 1873 economic depression turned Northern voters against further Southern intervention.
• Slaughter-House Cases (1873) narrowed the 14th Amendment’s reach.
• White-supremacist violence (Klan, White Leagues, Red Shirts) had already retaken most of the South before 1877.
• Internal Republican fatigue with Southern questions; Grant’s administration was distracted by scandal.
• Most Southern states had been ‘redeemed’ before the Compromise; 1877 ratified an existing reality.

Judgement: the Compromise of 1877 was the formal endpoint, but the deeper causes — depression, Court rulings, violence and political fatigue — had hollowed out Reconstruction first; a top-band answer reaches a clear verdict on cause vs symptom.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1996 study of US federalism):
‘The end of Reconstruction was not really about troops or terror at all. It was about the federal-state balance. The Slaughter-House Cases of 1873 narrowed the 14th Amendment, the United States v. Cruikshank decision in 1876 stripped its enforcement powers, and by 1877 the constitutional retreat was already complete. The withdrawal of soldiers was the symptom, not the cause.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation E.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘federal-state balance’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Slaughter-House, Cruikshank, retreat already complete); supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• Slaughter-House Cases (1873) narrowed the 14th Amendment’s Privileges and Immunities Clause.
• United States v. Cruikshank (1876) ruled that the federal government could not prosecute private actors for civil-rights violations.
• These rulings limited federal enforcement BEFORE the 1877 troop withdrawal.
• Most Southern states were ‘redeemed’ by 1875 — legal retreat preceded military retreat.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Federal troops had still been doing real protective work in South Carolina and Louisiana up to 1877.
• Klan violence required physical, not just legal, federal response.
• The Compromise of 1877 was followed by a sharp deterioration in Black voting rights, suggesting troops had mattered.
• Violence and law worked together; separating them gives a partial picture.

Judgement: E correctly draws attention to the constitutional retreat, but a top-band answer notes that the troop withdrawal mattered as a guarantee in its own right.

before.exam_tip_html: For an 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, the most common student error on this topic is conflating carpetbaggers with the Klan. Examiners reward precise definitions: carpetbaggers and scalawags were Republicans, the Klan attacked them. Use that precision to evaluate the interpretation’s specific argument. For 4-mark ‘Why Interpretations Differ’, focus on author purpose, evidence used and time of writing — especially the contrast between early-20th-century ‘Lost Cause’ histories and post-1960s revisionist work like Foner. You do NOT need to name historians.
before.content_html:
Three Labels That Are Easy to Get Wrong

Three groups dominate the Reconstruction story in the South: carpetbaggers, scalawags and the Ku Klux Klan. The three are constantly confused. The first two are political labels for Republican supporters of Reconstruction. The third is a terror group that targeted them. Untangling the labels is the foundation of any top-band answer on this topic.

Key Fact

Carpetbaggers were Northern Republicans who moved South after 1865. Scalawags were Southern white Republicans who backed Reconstruction. The Ku Klux Klan was a white-supremacist group founded by Confederate veterans in 1866 to attack BOTH groups, plus their Black political allies. The Klan was NOT founded by carpetbaggers.

Carpetbaggers in Reality

Around 50,000 Northerners moved to the South during Reconstruction. The label ‘carpetbagger’ was applied dismissively by Southern Democrats who claimed these incomers carried everything they owned in a cheap carpet bag — the implication being that they had nothing to lose and everything to plunder. Modern historians, especially Eric Foner and Lawrence Powell, have shown the cliche is largely false. Most carpetbaggers were professionals: teachers (many of them women working in Freedmen’s Bureau schools), Union army veterans seeking economic opportunity, lawyers, ministers and businessmen investing in the cotton recovery. Some served in Reconstruction state governments and were genuinely committed to multiracial democracy. A minority were corrupt, but the majority were not.

Scalawags: Native Southern Republicans

Scalawags were native white Southerners — many of them yeoman farmers from upland regions like east Tennessee, north Alabama and western North Carolina that had opposed secession in 1861. They joined the Republican Party for a mix of reasons: hostility to the planter class, support for federal infrastructure and education funding, and acceptance of emancipation. The label was a Southern insult borrowed from Scots dialect for a worthless animal. Scalawags were essential to Republican electoral success in the South: without them, Reconstruction governments would have rested on Black voters and carpetbaggers alone.

The Klan was founded in Pulaski, Tennessee, in late 1865 or early 1866 by six Confederate veterans, originally as a fraternal social club. By 1867 it had been militarised into a white-supremacist terror organisation under former Confederate general Nathan Bedford Forrest as its first Grand Wizard. Klansmen wore hooded white robes to hide their identities, attacked Black voters, schoolteachers and Republican politicians, and burned schools and freedpeople’s churches. By 1870 they were active across nearly every Southern state. Estimates of Klan-linked killings during the late 1860s and early 1870s run into the thousands.

Federal Response: The Enforcement Acts

Congress and President Grant moved against the Klan with three laws known together as the Enforcement Acts. The first (1870) made interference with voting rights a federal crime. The second (1870) put federal supervisors over congressional elections. The third (April 1871, the Ku Klux Klan Act) authorised the President to use federal troops, suspend habeas corpus and bring conspiracy charges. Grant invoked it in nine South Carolina counties in 1871; thousands of Klansmen were indicted, hundreds tried, and the original Klan was largely broken by 1872. Crucially, however, white-supremacist violence simply moved into looser organisations — the White Leagues of Louisiana, the Red Shirts of South Carolina and Mississippi.

Federal Retreat and the Compromise of 1877

Federal will faded after 1873. An economic depression that year sharpened Northern concern about taxes and turned Republican voters against further Southern intervention. The Supreme Court’s 1873 Slaughter-House Cases narrowed the reach of the 14th Amendment’s Privileges and Immunities Clause. By 1875 most Southern states had been ‘redeemed’ — that is, retaken by white Democratic governments calling themselves Redeemers. Only South Carolina, Louisiana and Florida still had Republican governments by 1876.

The 1876 presidential election was so close it triggered a constitutional crisis. Republican Rutherford B. Hayes and Democrat Samuel J. Tilden each claimed victory, with three Southern states’ results disputed. The unwritten Compromise of 1877 awarded the disputed electoral votes to Hayes; in return, Hayes withdrew the last federal troops from the South. Reconstruction ended.

With federal troops gone, Southern state legislatures gradually built a system of racial segregation and disfranchisement known as Jim Crow. Literacy tests, poll taxes and grandfather clauses cut the registered Black vote in Mississippi from around 130,000 in 1880 to under 1,000 by 1900. The Supreme Court’s Plessy v. Ferguson decision (1896) gave constitutional cover to ‘separate but equal’. The federal government would not seriously revisit the question for another sixty years. The Compromise of 1877 was therefore not just an end to Reconstruction but a long-term tilt of the federal-state balance back toward state control of civil rights.

Key Fact

Federal action against the Klan peaked with the 1870-71 Enforcement Acts, which Grant used decisively in South Carolina in 1871. After 1873’s economic depression and the Slaughter-House Cases, Northern political will faded. The Compromise of 1877 awarded Hayes the presidency in exchange for withdrawing federal troops, ending Reconstruction.

lessons.title: Homesteaders, Railroads and the Closing Frontier

practice_questions.text:
‘The Homestead Act was the main reason the Great Plains were settled between 1862 and 1890.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider the Homestead Act and other reasons.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that weighs the Homestead Act against other factors and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, dry farming, transcontinental railroad, open range).
Secure: Clear argument with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of multiple causes with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of the Homestead Act with little engagement with the ‘main reason’ framing.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (Homestead Act was main reason):
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims filed between 1862 and 1900 — the largest single redistribution of public land in US history.
• 160-acre quarter sections shaped the geography of Plains farming for generations.
• Federal land was free at a moment when Eastern land was scarce and expensive.

Challenging the statement (other factors mattered more):
• Pacific Railroad Act 1862 and the 1869 transcontinental railroad opened the Plains physically and advertised them.
• Around 175 million acres of railroad land grants — railroads were larger landowners than the Homestead Act’s claimants.
• New technologies (steel plough, windmills, dry farming, drought-resistant wheat, barbed wire) were what made the Plains farmable.
• Push factors: post-Civil War unemployment, European famine and persecution drove emigration.
• High failure rate: more than half of homestead claims were abandoned, suggesting the Act alone was not enough.

Judgement: the Homestead Act was the legal framework, but it would not have settled the Plains alone — the railroads, technology and immigration were equally indispensable; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict on this combination.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the completion of the transcontinental railroad in 1869 on the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two clearly developed effects with precise factual detail and clear distinction between strands of impact.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some support.
Developing: One effect developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of the railroad without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Cut journey time across the continent from around six months to about a week, transforming migration costs.
• Allowed Texas longhorn cattle to be moved by rail from cowtowns like Abilene to Eastern markets, creating the cattle boom of the 1870s.
• Accelerated the destruction of the buffalo herds — railroad construction crews and tourist hunters killed millions, with herds fragmented by the line itself.
• Made the Plains nations militarily isolatable — the US Army could move troops along the line in days rather than months.
• Drew European immigrants to the Plains via railroad-marketing offices in Sweden, Germany and Britain.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of barbed wire (patented by Joseph Glidden in 1874) on the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; engages with both farmer and rancher perspectives.
Secure: Two relevant effects with some support.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of barbed wire without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Allowed homesteaders to fence 160-acre claims cheaply for the first time, protecting crops from drifting cattle.
• Closed the open range, ending the era of long cattle drives north from Texas.
• Triggered the ‘fence-cutting wars’ in Texas and elsewhere as ranchers attacked homesteader fences in the late 1870s.
• Concentrated cattle ranching on smaller, fed and fenced operations — investment shifted from herd size to ranch infrastructure.
• Disrupted Plains nations’ remaining hunting routes by carving up grassland with new fences.

practice_questions.text:
‘Without the railroads, the Homestead Act would have had little effect on the Great Plains.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider the railroads and the Homestead Act.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; deploys specialist vocabulary; precise on both factors.
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement:
• Without rail, settlers could not move bulk crops to market — making 160-acre farms commercially viable.
• Railroad-funded immigration agents recruited the European settlers who took up much of the homestead land.
• Railroad land sales (175 million acres of grants) accounted for a vast share of Plains settlement, often alongside homestead claims.
• Railroads supplied the timber, machinery and barbed wire that made the Plains farmable.

Challenging the statement:
• The Homestead Act provided the legal mechanism for land transfer that no railroad could replicate.
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims testify to the Act’s independent reach.
• Many homesteaders settled on land miles from any rail line, surviving by older means.
• Push factors (Civil War dislocation, European persecution) operated independently of either factor.

Judgement: the railroads and the Homestead Act worked as a system; isolating one is artificial. A top-band answer concludes that they were complementary, with railroads more important for commercial viability and the Act more important for legal access.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of the winter of 1886-87 (the ‘Big Die-Up’) on the cattle industry of the Great Plains.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; engages with both immediate and structural consequences.
Secure: Two relevant effects.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of the winter without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• Killed up to nine-tenths of cattle in some northern ranges, wiping out years of accumulated wealth in months.
• Bankrupted many British and Eastern ranching syndicates, ending the boom in absentee ownership.
• Forced surviving ranchers onto smaller, fenced operations with stored winter feed.
• Combined with barbed wire to end the open-range era; Texas-to-Kansas long drives ceased.
• Concentrated ranching on more capital-intensive, smaller-herd operations that survived into the 20th century.

practice_questions.text: Explain the effects of new technology (steel plough, windmill, dry farming) on Plains agriculture between 1860 and 1890.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Two developed effects with precise factual detail; clearly distinguishes specific technologies.
Secure: Two relevant effects.
Developing: One developed and one weak.
Emerging: Description of technology without focus on effects.

Indicative content:
• John Deere’s steel plough cut through Plains sod that had broken Eastern iron ploughs — making fields cultivatable for the first time.
• Windmill-pumped wells reached deep aquifers, providing reliable water for stock and households where surface water was scarce.
• Dry farming techniques (breaking up soil after rain, leaving fallow alternate years) raised yields in low-rainfall areas like the Dakotas.
• Drought-resistant Russian wheat, brought by Mennonite immigrants, made wheat farming reliable in Kansas.
• Together these technologies extended the ‘line of farms’ west of the 100th meridian, into land that had been unfarmable a generation earlier.

before.exam_tip_html: For a 12-mark Period Essay on settlement, the strongest answers refuse the ‘Homestead Act success story’ cliche. Engage explicitly with the failure rate and the role of the railroads in advertising AND profiting from the same land Congress had given them. For an 8-mark Explain Effects, split the impact into clear strands — on settlers, on the cattle industry, on the Plains nations — and develop two strands rather than skimming all three. Specialist vocabulary (sod-buster, dry farming, open range, Big Die-Up) gains marks under SPaG.
before.content_html:
The Two 1862 Acts That Made the West

In May and July 1862, with most Southern Democrats absent from Congress, the Republican-dominated Senate and House passed two laws that would remake the West. The Homestead Act offered 160 acres of public land to any head of household who lived on it for five years and paid a small fee. The Pacific Railroad Act granted federal land and bonds to two companies — the Union Pacific and the Central Pacific — to build a transcontinental rail line. Together the two laws aimed to fill the Great Plains with farming families and bind the nation by iron rail.

Key Fact

Under the 1862 Homestead Act, a settler could claim 160 acres (a quarter section) of public land for an $18 filing fee. To gain title they had to live on the land, build a dwelling and cultivate crops for five continuous years.

Why the Headline Hides the Failure Rate

The Homestead Act became a founding myth of the American West — free land for any family with the courage to claim it. The reality was harsher. Around 1.6 million homestead claims were filed between 1862 and 1900; more than half were abandoned before the five years were up. On the dry High Plains, 160 acres was simply too small to support a family without irrigation. Drought, debt, isolation, plagues of grasshoppers and prairie fires drove most homestead families either to sell up to neighbours or to give up and leave. Engaging with this failure rate is what separates a top-band answer from a textbook recall.

The Transcontinental Railroad

Construction on the transcontinental railroad began in 1863 and finished on 10 May 1869, when the Union Pacific (building west from Omaha, Nebraska) met the Central Pacific (building east from Sacramento, California) at Promontory Point, Utah. A golden spike marked the joining. The line cut a journey across the continent from six months by wagon to about a week by train. Federal land grants to the railroad companies were vast: by 1871 around 175 million acres of public land had been granted to railroads — an area larger than Texas. Railroads then sold this land at a profit to the very settlers homesteading nearby.

Railroad companies were not just transport providers — they were marketers of the West. They sent agents to Northern Europe and to the Eastern states with pamphlets and posters promising fertile land and a healthy climate. Northern Pacific brochures advertising the Dakotas appeared in Sweden, Norway, Germany and Britain in five different languages. By 1890 around a quarter of homestead claims came from immigrant families. Railroads ran subsidised emigrant trains carrying settlers and their goods west at low fares — on the calculation that filled-up land along the line meant freight to ship in both directions.

Farming Problems on the Plains

The Great Plains punished settlers used to Eastern conditions. Annual rainfall west of the 100th meridian was less than 20 inches — below the threshold for traditional grain farming. Timber was scarce; settlers built homes from cut-out blocks of prairie turf and were nicknamed sod-busters. The thick grass roots blunted ordinary cast-iron ploughs. Grasshopper plagues, the worst in 1874-75, stripped entire fields in hours. Prairie fires, often started by lightning or sparks from passing trains, swept across hundreds of miles. Winter blizzards killed cattle and isolated families for weeks. Children walked miles to one-room schools when weather allowed.

Solutions: New Tools, New Methods

Settler ingenuity and industrial invention combined to make the Plains farmable. John Deere’s steel plough (improved through the 1860s) cut through tough sod that broke iron blades. Wind-powered pumps lifted water from deep aquifers. Dry farming techniques broke up the soil after each rain to trap moisture, leaving fields fallow in alternate years. Drought-resistant Russian Turkey Red wheat, brought by Mennonite immigrants from the steppe, transformed yields in Kansas and the Dakotas. Joseph Glidden’s 1874 patent for cheap, mass-producible barbed wire finally let homesteaders fence their fields against drifting cattle — the open range began to close.

From the late 1860s, Texas longhorn cattle were driven north along the Chisholm Trail to railhead cowtowns such as Abilene, Dodge City and Wichita. Joseph McCoy turned Abilene into the first cowtown in 1867. The herds grazed for free on the unfenced grassland of the Great Plains — the ‘open range’. Eastern and British investors poured money into ranch syndicates, expecting easy returns. The system collapsed in two stages. First, barbed wire enclosed the range from the mid-1870s. Then, the savage winter of 1886-87 — the ‘Big Die-Up’ — killed up to nine-tenths of cattle in some northern ranges. By 1890 the open range was over; cattle ranching survived on a smaller, fenced and fed scale.

Key Fact

The four big farming problems on the Plains were lack of timber, lack of water, tough sod and crop failure from drought or pests. The four big solutions were sod homes, windmill-pumped wells, John Deere’s steel plough and dry farming with drought-resistant wheat. Barbed wire (1874) closed the open range.

lessons.title: Little Bighorn, Wounded Knee and the End of the Frontier

practice_questions.text:
‘The 1887 Dawes Act had a greater impact on the Plains nations than the Battle of the Little Bighorn.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider the Dawes Act and the Battle of the Little Bighorn.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained comparative argument with substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (allotment, annuity, reservation, Ghost Dance).
Secure: Clear comparison with relevant detail; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of one or both with little comparison.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (Dawes had greater impact):
• Dawes Act reduced tribal landholding from around 138 million acres to 48 million between 1887 and 1934 — a two-thirds loss.
• Forced cultural assimilation: removal of children to boarding schools where Indigenous languages were forbidden.
• Allotment broke up communal landholding traditions; ‘surplus’ land went to white settlement.
• Long-term: shaped tribal poverty and land tenure for the entire 20th century.

Challenging the statement (Little Bighorn had greater impact):
• Symbolic power of the most spectacular Native victory of the Plains wars.
• Provoked the federal response that broke Lakota military independence by 1881.
• Led directly to the surrender of Crazy Horse and the exile of Sitting Bull.
• Triggered the campaign of cultural and territorial reduction that the Dawes Act later codified.

Judgement: Little Bighorn was decisive militarily but Dawes was the deeper, longer-lasting blow; a top-band answer reaches an explicit verdict and substantiates it. A nuanced answer notes the two are connected: Dawes only became politically possible because the Plains nations had been militarily defeated.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation A and Interpretation B.

Interpretation A (from a 1900 popular American history written for a general readership):
‘The closing of the frontier in 1890 was the climax of the American story. Brave pioneers had crossed a continent, civilisation had triumphed over wilderness, and the United States stood ready to take its place among the great powers of the earth.’

Interpretation B (from a 1991 study of the American West):
‘The closing of the frontier in 1890 was the climax of a long process of conquest. The Plains nations were not a wilderness to be civilised but communities to be dispossessed. The Dawes Act, Wounded Knee and the 1890 Census report belong together as the formal end of that conquest.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation B. In your answer you should refer to Interpretation A and use your own knowledge.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of B’s ‘long process of conquest’ thesis; engages with specific claims (Plains nations as communities, Dawes Act, Wounded Knee, 1890 Census); contrasts with A; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation with reference to A; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the topic without engaging with B’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting B):
• Dawes Act 1887: reduction of tribal land from 138m to 48m acres.
• Wounded Knee Massacre, 29 December 1890: at least 250 Lakota killed.
• Buffalo destruction reducing herds from 30m to fewer than 1,000 by 1885 — deliberate federal weapon.
• Plains nations had complex political and economic life pre-1840 — not a ‘wilderness’.

Indicative content (qualifying B / supporting A):
• Settler experience was hard and many homesteaders died — the ‘triumphal’ framing reflects real human achievement.
• A speaks for the dominant late-19th-century American self-understanding (Turner Thesis).
• A’s framing is not factually wrong, just morally selective — a difference of emphasis.

Judgement: B is the stronger interpretation in light of modern evidence; a top-band answer notes A reflects the dominant national narrative of its own moment.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation C.

Interpretation C (from a 2005 study of US Indian policy):
‘The Dawes Act of 1887 was sold to the public as humanitarian reform. Senator Dawes himself believed allotment would lift Indigenous families out of poverty by giving them private property. The reality was the destruction of communal land tenure and the loss of two-thirds of remaining tribal land in fifty years. Good intentions did not change devastating outcomes.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation C.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of C’s ‘humanitarian intentions, devastating outcomes’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of the Dawes Act without engaging with C’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting C):
• Henry Dawes and his allies described the Act in humanitarian terms; the ‘Friends of the Indian’ lobby supported it.
• Tribal landholding fell from 138m acres to 48m between 1887 and 1934.
• Allotments often went to land too dry for family farming.
• Forced boarding-school removal devastated language and culture independent of land loss.

Indicative content (qualifying C):
• Some allotments were genuinely productive and family-supporting.
• Not all reformers were sincere; the Act had clear settler-colonial beneficiaries who expected ‘surplus’ land.
• Cultural impact was as devastating as economic impact — C focuses on land loss but boarding schools also need weighting.

Judgement: C captures the gap between framing and outcome accurately; a top-band answer notes that the cultural assault (boarding schools, language ban) was as important as the land loss the interpretation foregrounds.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation D.

Interpretation D (from a 1996 study of the Plains nations after 1850):
‘Wounded Knee was not the end of resistance — it was the moment outside observers stopped noticing it. Lakota communities continued to refuse allotment, hide ceremonies, and assert rights to the Black Hills throughout the 20th century. To call 1890 a closing is to use a settler calendar.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation D.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of D’s ‘continuing resistance’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of Wounded Knee without engaging with D’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting D):
• Lakota legal action over the Black Hills continued; the Supreme Court ruled in 1980 that the seizure had been unlawful.
• Continued resistance to allotment and language suppression in many tribal communities.
• ‘Closing of the frontier’ was a US Census definition with no equivalent meaning to the Plains nations.

Indicative content (qualifying D):
• Wounded Knee did mark the end of large-scale armed resistance.
• Federal control of reservations was effective from 1890.
• The 1890 framing is useful for understanding US policy even if not for understanding Lakota experience.

Judgement: D’s point is well-taken — resistance continued under different forms — but a top-band answer notes the closing of armed resistance was a real change, even if cultural and legal resistance continued.

practice_questions.text:
‘The closing of the frontier in 1890 was a national achievement.’

To what extent is this statement valid?

In your answer you should consider the case that it was an achievement and the case that it was a tragedy.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained argument that takes an explicit position on achievement vs tragedy and reaches a substantiated overall judgement; precise factual support; deploys specialist vocabulary (Manifest Destiny, allotment, Ghost Dance, Frontier Thesis).
Secure: Clear argument addressing both sides; judgement reached.
Developing: Coverage of both sides with limited weighing.
Emerging: Description of the closing of the frontier with no clear engagement with the ‘achievement’ framing.

Indicative content:
Supporting the statement (achievement):
• Continental nation united by transcontinental rail since 1869.
• Around 1.6 million homestead claims filed; the Plains transformed into a major agricultural region.
• Sectional civil war wounds beginning to heal under shared westward expansion.
• Industrial economy on track to overtake Britain’s by 1890.

Challenging the statement (tragedy):
• Plains nations dispossessed, buffalo destroyed (30m to fewer than 1,000), Wounded Knee Massacre (December 1890).
• Dawes Act reduced tribal land by two-thirds.
• Closing came at the cost of around 4 million people enslaved emancipated but trapped in sharecropping; Reconstruction overthrown by 1877.
• ‘Closing’ framing was a settler-perspective summary; Plains nations did not regard 1890 as a closure but as a moment of catastrophe.

Judgement: a defensible verdict can argue achievement OR tragedy OR both. The 12-mark band rewards an explicit, substantiated position. A top-band answer recognises the closing was both achievement (for one set of Americans) and catastrophe (for another), and weighs the two.

practice_questions.text:
Read Interpretation E.

Interpretation E (from a 1993 study of post-Civil War America):
‘Federal policy toward the Plains nations between 1867 and 1890 was strikingly consistent: confine, contain, and assimilate. Whether under Republican or Democratic administrations, the small reservations policy, the destruction of the buffalo, and the Dawes Act all served the same long aim.’

Evaluate the interpretation in Interpretation E.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering: Sustained evaluation of E’s ‘consistent policy’ thesis; engages with specific claims; supports judgement with precise own knowledge.
Secure: Clear evaluation; relevant own knowledge.
Developing: Some evaluation; partial own knowledge.
Emerging: Description of policy without engaging with E’s argument.

Indicative content (supporting E):
• 1867 Medicine Lodge and 1868 Fort Laramie Treaties established small reservations.
• Buffalo destruction was tolerated and encouraged across multiple administrations.
• 1887 Dawes Act under Republican Congress shared assumptions with the 1881 Helen Hunt Jackson’s ‘reform’ lobby.
• Bipartisan support for assimilationist boarding schools throughout the era.

Indicative content (qualifying E):
• Grant’s ‘Peace Policy’ (1869) attempted a more conciliatory approach via Quaker reservation agents — not identical to military containment.
• The Great Sioux War (1876-77) was a sharper military rupture than the ‘consistent’ framing implies.
• Some reformers (the ‘Friends of the Indian’) genuinely opposed harsher Western politicians.

Judgement: E captures real consistency in long-term aims but flattens significant differences in method and tone; a top-band answer concedes the underlying continuity while noting genuine variation in how it was pursued.

before.content_html:
From Treaties to Small Reservations

By the late 1860s the United States had abandoned the older policy of a Permanent Indian Frontier and shifted to a system of small reservations. The 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty placed the southern Plains nations — Comanche, Kiowa, Cheyenne and Arapaho — on reservations in present-day Oklahoma. The 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty placed the northern Plains Lakota on the Great Sioux Reservation in Dakota Territory, with the sacred Black Hills inside it. The treaties promised annuity goods (tools, food, blankets) and assured the nations that the Black Hills would belong to them ‘as long as the grass shall grow’.

Around the new reservations, federal policy attacked the buffalo herds on which Plains life depended. Railroad sport-hunters, hide hunters supplying Eastern leather factories, and the deliberate encouragement of military commanders like General Sheridan combined to reduce the buffalo from an estimated 30 million in 1860 to fewer than a thousand by 1885. Buffalo destruction was a Plains nations’ subsistence collapse and a federal weapon in the same act.

Key Fact

The 1867 Medicine Lodge Treaty placed southern Plains nations on Oklahoma reservations; the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty placed the Lakota on the Great Sioux Reservation, including the sacred Black Hills. Together they replaced earlier treaty territories with a system of fixed, smaller reservations.

Black Hills Gold and the Great Sioux War

In 1874 a US Army expedition led by Colonel George Custer confirmed gold in the Black Hills. Within a year miners poured in, breaking the 1868 Fort Laramie Treaty. When the federal government failed to remove them and offered to buy the Black Hills, the Lakota leaders — Sitting Bull and Crazy Horse foremost among them — refused. The army responded by ordering all Lakota onto the reservation by January 1876 or be treated as hostile. Most refused. The result was the Great Sioux War of 1876-77.

The Battle of the Little Bighorn, June 1876

On 25 June 1876, Lieutenant Colonel Custer’s Seventh Cavalry attacked a vast Lakota and Cheyenne encampment along the Little Bighorn River in Montana. Custer underestimated the camp’s size and split his command. Crazy Horse led the counter-charge; Custer and around 268 of his men were killed. The Battle of the Little Bighorn was the most spectacular Native victory of the Plains wars. It was also their last. The shock to American opinion drove Congress to pour troops into the region; within a year Crazy Horse had surrendered and was killed in custody, and Sitting Bull had taken his people into Canada (returning in 1881).

With the Plains nations militarily contained, federal policy shifted to forced cultural assimilation. The Dawes Act of 1887, named after Senator Henry Dawes, broke up tribal reservations into 160-acre family allotments — the same quarter sections homesteaders had been claiming since 1862. ‘Surplus’ reservation land was opened to white settlement. Citizenship was offered to those who accepted allotments and adopted ‘civilised’ ways. Children were taken from families and sent to off-reservation boarding schools where Indigenous languages were forbidden. Between 1887 and 1934 the Dawes system reduced tribal landholding from around 138 million acres to 48 million — a loss of two-thirds.

The Ghost Dance and Wounded Knee

In 1889 a Paiute prophet, Wovoka, had a vision: if Indigenous peoples lived peacefully and performed a ritual Ghost Dance, the dead would return, the buffalo would come back and white settlers would vanish. The movement spread quickly to the Lakota in 1890. Reservation agents, alarmed, called for troops. Sitting Bull was killed by reservation police on 15 December 1890. Two weeks later, on 29 December 1890, the Seventh Cavalry intercepted a band of Miniconjou Lakota under Spotted Elk at Wounded Knee Creek in South Dakota. As soldiers tried to disarm the band, a shot was fired; the cavalry opened up with rifles and Hotchkiss cannon. At least 250 Lakota men, women and children were killed. Twenty-five US soldiers died, many from their own crossfire.

The Frontier ‘Closes’

The 1890 US Census report contained a single sentence with vast cultural reach: it declared that there was no longer a continuous frontier line of unsettled territory. Three years later, the historian Frederick Jackson Turner read his Frontier Thesis at the World’s Columbian Exposition in Chicago. Turner argued that the experience of conquering the frontier had created American democracy itself; with the frontier closed, a defining era of American history was over. Turner’s thesis dominated Western history for most of the 20th century.

From the 1980s onwards, revisionist historians like Patricia Nelson Limerick and Richard White rejected Turner’s triumphalism. Limerick’s Legacy of Conquest (1987) reframed the West as a story of conquest, race and unfinished business rather than progress. White’s work foregrounded Native agency — treating the Plains nations as active negotiators and adapters, not passive victims. The two views are not symmetrical: most modern historians broadly accept the revisionist case while debating its emphasis. Examiners do not require students to name these historians, but the IDEAS — conquest vs progress, agency vs victimhood — are valuable for top-band interpretation answers.

Key Fact

The closing of the frontier rests on four milestones in close sequence: the 1887 Dawes Act, the December 1890 Wounded Knee Massacre, the 1890 Census declaration that the frontier no longer existed, and Frederick Jackson Turner’s 1893 Frontier Thesis. Whether the closing was a national achievement, a tragedy or both is the central historical debate.

For an 8-mark Evaluate an Interpretation, engage with the SPECIFIC argument of the interpretation, not the general topic. The Turner-vs-Limerick framing supplies useful flavour but you do not need to name historians.
